application: Sponsors and properties using marketability rankings should check the method and add their own audience and fit data.
limitations: Largely commentary on a third-party list; the method critique is Schiffer's, summarised briefly.
title: Who are the most marketable female athletes in the world?
role: Editor, The Boston Globe; author, The Fixture
summary: McInerney looks at SportsPro's 2026 list of the 50 most marketable athletes, built with NorthStar Solutions Group: 16 women made it, down from 20 last year and 23 in 2023, led by Aryna Sabalenka at No. 1. She flags Jessica Schiffer's critique that counting the deals an athlete signs measures how fast their sponsorship business is growing rather than real brand demand, which is why Coco Gauff sits at 32. Her reading: tennis dominates on global appeal, cricket's Smriti Mandhana (15 million-plus Instagram followers) and Jemimah Rodrigues rank ahead of LA28, and no American women's soccer player is in the top 150.
why: A useful caution on how athlete marketability rankings are built before using them to price or pick talent deals.

application: Rights holders can copy the creator deep-link model and price new in-app live surfaces as sponsor inventory.
limitations: The 30 million figure is the league's claim; the forecasts on virtual-camera ad inventory and a consumer smart ball are the author's.
title: NBA 2026/27 Innovation Review
role: Founder, FutureSport Co; former lead, City Fan Labs (City Football Group)
summary: Farren reviews three NBA innovation stories for the new season: Amazon's Prime 360 virtual camera system built on AWS Trainium and gaussian splatting, the NBA app's upgrades (Tap to Watch links on TikTok posts tagged #NBA and on creator highlights, Game Pulse live court tracking with AI catch-ups, the Ask NBA chatbot), and a blind test of a sensor ball that Adam Silver says could be used in officiating as soon as 2027/28. He compares the ball with the NFL's Zebra chips, FIFA's Adidas sensor and LaLiga's Kinexon ball now used in every match. His takeaways: the league says Tap to Watch drove 30 million fans to live games last season, the creator links are distribution with a conversion mechanic for the price of a rights waiver, and Game Pulse is unsponsored live in-app inventory.
why: Shows a league using creators, search and its own app to turn casual clip viewers into live viewers while keeping the fan relationship and data.

application: Rights holders growing audiences in emerging markets can plan for the point where scale converts to higher-value revenue and own the distribution layer early.
limitations: Preliminary findings ahead of client reports; the charts behind the figures were not in the public text.
title: Culture shock: What 10,500 labels reveal about the Global South's genre story
role: Managing Director, MIDiA Research
summary: Mulligan previews a new MIDiA dataset mapping 10,500 record labels by country, revenue, genre and distributor. Global South genres (Afrobeats, amapiano, K-pop, sertanejo and others) hold about a fifth of revenue, streams and labels, but a higher share of labels than revenue, and in regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa and MENA revenue share can be more than three times smaller than stream share; their labels also export five times less music than US and European labels. He expects subscriber growth in Brazil, Mexico and India to close the streams-to-revenue gap and local scale to push these genres into Western charts, and says distribution is the one scalable answer for Western rightsholders, citing Believe, which distributes about half of the Turkish labels in the dataset.
why: Shows how audience growth in lower-value markets turns into revenue and competition later, and who captures it.

application: Commercial teams can add governance and community-risk checks to sponsor due diligence and build first-party audience proof to sell to brands that already fit their fans.
limitations: Supporter backlash and the motives behind Firmus's deals are the author's reading; the 20% community-spend clause is his proposal, not an industry norm.
title: Firmus $44B Shorts: Australia’s wobbling AI sports and social gambit
role: Writes The Black Book; former head of Australasia for Bleacher Report/TNT Sports, interim media and communications manager for SANZAAR and CMO of BLK Sport
summary: Mortimer uses AI data centre company Firmus, which signed a six-year Foundation Major Partner deal on the Tasmania Devils' playing shorts plus deals with Cricket Tasmania, the JackJumpers and the Hobart Jewels, then pulled a float meant to value it at about $44 billion, as a case study in AI becoming sport's next 'legitimacy buyer' after tobacco, alcohol, gambling and crypto. He sets it beside NextDC losing 41.7% of its value in one session after residents blocked power lines for its Melbourne M3 site, and argues infrastructure sponsors are trying to rent social licence that a jersey cannot supply. Citing Ben Wells of PTI Digital, he says clubs keep taking reputational-risk money because they cannot prove first-party audience value to category-aligned brands, and proposes sponsor due diligence, real fan data and contracted local community spend.
why: A sharp case for why rights holders that cannot prove audience value end up selling their most visible inventory to whichever sector needs to buy legitimacy.

application: Clubs can define which questions they will answer at principle level (pricing, access, strategy) and commit to returning to them, rather than defaulting to silence.
limitations: An insider's view of ownership; it offers no evidence on how supporters respond to this kind of communication.
title: 📬 Fans First: Why Not Every Club Decision Can Be Public
role: Founder, Berkida Ventures; The Berkida Brief
summary: Marinelli, a former Leeds United board member who sits on AC Monza's board, argues that more institutional capital in sport should raise the bar for owner accountability, but that putting fans first does not mean making every transfer target, budget or internal dispute public. He explains how disclosure can raise transfer costs and why squad-cost rules (UEFA's 70% limit and the Premier League's 85% ratio from 2026/27) mean a willing shareholder cannot simply spend more. He sets out what supporters should expect instead: a clear strategy, honest broad finances, regular forums that get real answers, principles on ticket pricing and access, and fuller explanations once circumstances allow.
why: A practical framework for how club owners can be accountable to supporters without damaging negotiations.

application: Relevant to anyone weighing public, private-equity or family ownership for a rights holder or entertainment business.
limitations: An opinion piece written before UMG's Q3 results; the take-private talks are reported, not confirmed.
title: 🔵 Universal wants out... but can it pull that off?
role: Founder and MD, Motive Unknown (music marketing agency, UK); Network Notes
summary: Hemmings argues Universal Music Group's senior redundancies and reported interest in a private-equity-backed take-private are about a mismatch with public investors, not weak profitability. He links the slide (shares down 33.8% at 15 Oct) to Bill Ackman's complaints that UMG would not publish capital allocation plans or take on debt for growth, which ended with Pershing Square selling out. Until UMG finds a sympathetic private backer, he expects more margin-driven cuts that could weaken marketing and distribution for the artists and labels that rely on it, and leave it open to a less friendly buyer.
why: A sharp read on how ownership structure and investor expectations shape the operating choices of a dominant entertainment company.

application: A case for testing exclusivity decisions against reach and engagement data rather than core-fan applause.
limitations: Short-term monthly data; the book and accessibility segments are not covered here.
title: Wolverine lifts PS5, but Xbox struggles despite Gears of War launch
role: Leads The Game Business; previously nine years at MCV and over eight years as head of GamesIndustry.biz
summary: Dring's edition uses Circana analyst Mat Piscatella's data to show Marvel's Wolverine, not the GTA 6 reveal, lifted PS5 in September: US revenue up 43% and UK units up 24%, with the Wolverine DualSense the month's bestselling accessory. Xbox hardware fell 22% in the UK in October and Piscatella sees no lift from the Gears of War exclusive or disc-to-digital programme, while pulling Call of Duty from Game Pass cost engagement with no benefit. Switch 2 US revenue was down 12% after a price rise handled by dropping a bundle at the same shelf price.
why: Hard sales data on whether exclusives and subscription changes actually move a platform, a question every rights-led business faces.

application: A reminder that local identity can be a commercial asset worth protecting when chasing international talent.
limitations: Short and based on public reporting; no new financial data.
title: What the Collapse of ENCE and Evil Geniuses Really Means for Esports
role: Esports and gaming marketing agency founder; lecturer; 20+ years in esports
summary: Decker pushes back on the idea that the shutdown of ENCE and Evil Geniuses within a week proves esports is broken. He says EG was badly mismanaged from 2019 to 2023 and lost players, fans and sponsors, while ENCE, profitable from 2020 to 2023 per Ilta-Sanomat, lost its home-market standing when it dropped its all-Finnish Counter-Strike roster and ran up $1.8 million in losses across 2024 and 2025. His frame is that esports teams are startups, and some fail.
why: A useful corrective on reading two failures as a market verdict, with the specific causes behind each.

application: Rights holders selling star access to fans and brands in politically sensitive markets need contract terms, market-specific briefing and a response plan before a crisis, not after.
limitations: The image-rights exposure is the author's reasoning; he says he does not know whether the cancelled deals fall under that arrangement or their value.
title: Athletes, China and the Commercial Cost of Speaking Freely For Mbappé
role: Founder and publisher, Faze 3 Sport; Culture of Sport and Original Football
summary: Skilling traces how one off-the-cuff Mbappé remark about a Mao Zedong meme cost him three Chinese sponsors (Dongpeng, Mengniu, Milkground) and led China Media Group to suspend CCTV coverage of La Liga, pulling Real Madrid and Javier Tebas into public apologies. He sets out Madrid's exposure: about 97 million supporters in China per Nielsen data the club has cited, a reported 10% to 15% of international merchandise revenue, Chinese partners such as Hisense and Roborock, and a reported 80/20 image-rights split that could give the club a direct interest in some lost deals. His point is that a single player's comment can become a league-wide broadcast and sponsorship problem, which explains why clubs keep player media so tightly scripted.
why: Shows how athlete-led international growth creates concentrated commercial risk that spreads to clubs, leagues and their partners.

application: A model for rights holders building a connected fan ecosystem across content, membership, merchandise and events.
limitations: Written to promote the podcast episode, and the author has a commercial tie to Hallmark.
title: Hallmark’s Billion-Minute Fandom
role: Media cartographer; Media War & Peace; co-host The Media Odyssey; former network executive
summary: Shapiro argues Hallmark's fandom comes from a tight, unchanging brand promise of positivity and comfort, which lets it stretch into many business lines its team calls One Hallmark. He lists 100 movies a year (40 of them holiday films), more than 1,100 stores, distribution in 146 countries, the Hallmark+ streaming service, a new YouTube channel, a FAST channel, a Christmas cruise with Norwegian that sells out in hours with a 70,000-person waitlist, and a Kansas City Christmas Experience drawing more than 100,000 people. He contrasts this with serial subscriber churn at brands whose viewers are loyal to shows, not to the brand. Shapiro discloses he produced a Hallmark film last year.
why: Shows how a clear brand identity can carry fans from screen to membership, retail and live events.

application: Useful when weighing a single-face launch strategy against a broader athlete roster.
limitations: Only the free opening is readable; the rest of the analysis sits behind the paywall.
title: Why the Mbappé-China Scandal Is Bad News for On and Real Madrid
role: Founder and writer, Sportsverse; award-winning business journalist
summary: Summary based on public excerpt. Miller looks at the Mbappé China backlash from the side of On, the Swiss sportswear brand he joined in September after ending a 20-year Nike partnership to front its football launch. Within 24 hours Mengniu Dairy, Shanghai Milkground and Eastroc dropped him and Chinese platforms restricted his accounts, per Reuters, and On's stock was down 8% over five days by Wednesday's pre-market trading as investors priced in guilt by association.
why: A concrete case of how a single athlete's misstep can hit a brand partner's valuation, not just its marketing.

title: New Episode of BBOC: Syracuse University Director of Athletics Bryan Blair
role: Founder and CEO, JohnWallStreet
summary: On Big Business on Campus, Corey Leff and Playfly Sports chairman Michael Schreiber talk to Syracuse athletic director Bryan Blair about funding growth through fundraising, premium seating and youth sports, per the episode write-up in the JohnWallStreet email.
why: Practical examples of turning facilities, participants and local growth into premium and ticketing revenue.
key_points: Blair treats fundraising as a maths problem: more staff and more asks, and says college sport cannot cut its way to prosperity.
Only 3% to 4% of the Dome's seats are tied to a suite or club; regional growth after Micron's $100 billion investment could support 15% to 20%.
At Toledo he ran the first youth league operated by a Division I athletic department, a six-figure revenue line before concessions and parking, with student athletes paid as coaches for NIL income.
Registrant data was to feed the ticketing funnel: free tickets for the kids, paid tickets for their families.

application: A frame for pitching live and community products to investors, and for spotting where capital is heading.
limitations: A thesis piece that promotes the author's own fund and community, with little data beyond one survey.
title: The Offline Economy (and why it’s where the next great companies will be built)
role: Founder and GP, Profluence (Profluence Capital)
summary: Petcash sets out Profluence's investment thesis that AI makes digital content abundant and pushes value toward trust, community and live experiences, which he calls the Offline Economy. He cites a Live Nation study (93% crave real experiences over digital, 80% would rather spend on experiences than things), argues sports act as a wedge into adjacent markets such as wellness, collectibles and travel, and says infrastructure and software under the industry are underbuilt compared with franchises and media rights.
why: A compact version of an investor's case for why AI could raise the value of live sport and community.

title: THE SECRET TO HALLMARK'S BILLION-MINUTE FANDOM
role: Media cartographer; Media War & Peace; co-host The Media Odyssey; former network executive
summary: Recorded live at MIPCOM, Evan Shapiro and Marion Ranchet interview Jon Sichel, Hallmark Media's head of distribution, on how a 116-year-old family-owned brand moves fans across TV, streaming, retail and live events, per the episode's published takeaways.
why: A clear example of streaming membership used as the hub of a wider fan ecosystem.
key_points: Hallmark Movies on YouTube, launched October 2025, has had 84 million views and about 2.6 billion minutes watched, with a younger audience than TV.

YouTube viewers are pointed to Hallmark+, which bundles store discounts, free cards, e-cards and access to events like the 100,000-visitor Kansas City Christmas Experience: more membership than subscription.
About 100 films a year, roughly 40 holiday titles, each shot in two to three weeks on tight budgets and tax credits.
Selective licensing to Netflix and Peacock is used to bring fans back to Hallmark's own platforms; it operates in 145 countries and takes Hallmark+ abroad next.
Sichel credits private family ownership, free of quarterly Wall Street reporting, for its reinvestment culture.

application: A prompt to stress-test international partner and broadcast deals for talent and reputation risk.
limitations: The author says he does not know whether the lost deals fall under the image-rights split or their remaining value.
title: Mbappé, China and the Commercial Cost of Speaking Freely
role: Founder and publisher, Faze 3 Sport; Culture of Sport and Original Football
summary: Skilling traces how Mbappe's off-the-cuff Mao meme comment cost him three Chinese sponsors (Dongpeng, Mengniu, Milkground) and led CCTV's parent to suspend La Liga coverage, forcing apologies from Mbappe, Javier Tebas and Real Madrid. He puts the exposure in numbers: Madrid cites about 97 million supporters in China, which reportedly supplies 10 to 15% of its international merchandise revenue, and Mbappe reportedly gives the club 20% of certain image-rights income. His point is that one player's remark can hit a whole league's broadcast and sponsor base, which is why clubs script what players say.
why: Shows how one player's comment can spread into league-wide media rights and sponsorship risk in a key international market.

application: A lens for sport and live businesses on how to fund talent and IP without taking the asset, for example athlete or creator partnerships.
limitations: Opinion from an artist manager with a clear stake; the proposed vehicle is a concept, not a tested model.
title: The Next Great Music Company Won't Be a Record Label
role: Toronto-based artist manager and sync rep; co-founder of Sincerely Management, Fivepin Music and Sellout.fm; writes The Artist Economy
summary: Gouveia argues the traditional record deal combines the worst of debt and equity: artists repay advances out of a 15 to 20% royalty, so a record must gross 5 to 6 times the advance to recoup, while the label keeps the master forever. He cites Citigroup's finding that artists got about 12% of the US$43 billion US music business in 2017, majors cutting costs and A&R staff, and catalogue now at 75% of US streams, so labels sign only proven acts. His answer is an anti-label vehicle that applies staged venture logic: investors share in growth, artists keep their copyrights and can buy investors out.
why: A sharp breakdown of how the music industry's core financing model works and why capital may shift from ownership to staged investment in talent.

application: Context for anyone tracking multi-club owner exits and buyer depth in football.
limitations: Largely compiled from other outlets' reporting, with light original analysis.
title: India’s Rs 1,857 crore bat-and-ball bet
role: Founder, The State of Play; The Left Field
summary: Ananth details India's Rs 1,856.67 crore Khelo India sports goods scheme to 2033-34: four manufacturing zones, Rs 1,130 crore in anchor and turnover-linked incentives, and Rs 105 crore to cover certification costs, with no export or jobs target set. He also explains why INEOS (about GBP18 billion in debt) is selling Lausanne-Sport and Nice and why Friedkin is testing a controlling-stake sale of Everton less than two years after buying it, noting the shortage of bidders at the GBP1 billion level.
why: A quick, numbers-led read on the owner retreat in European football and India's push to build a sports goods industry.

application: A reminder for leagues and investors to plan for concentrated ownership risk and broaden their capital base.
limitations: Built on a Bloomberg report; the sale and price are not confirmed.
title: Mark Walter’s potential sale of the Los Angeles Sparks could rock women’s sports
role: Editor, The Boston Globe; author, The Fixture
summary: McInerney looks at Bloomberg's report that Mark Walter, under federal investigation and already seller of the Lakers for US$12.5 billion, wants about US$700 million for the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks, including a roughly US$150 million training centre opening in 2027. That would more than double the US$300 million record set for the Connecticut Sun. Her bigger worry is the PWHL, which Walter founded and bankrolls: it has doubled in size with no media-rights deal yet, and its first outside investors (Ilitch, and Kilmer with a reported US$100 million) may need to step up if he exits.
why: A useful read on women's sports valuations and the risk of a league relying on one principal backer.

title: Highlight: The Real Math Behind a $30B Lakers Valuation
role: Founder, Navigate (sport and entertainment strategy and valuation); host, Navigating Sports Business
summary: In a short highlight, Navigate founder AJ Maestas explains how a Lakers franchise that sold for US$12.5 billion could be projected at US$30 billion in ten years, arguing these sales were never really about fundamentals, per the episode notes. He compares buying a franchise to buying a Picasso and says the open question is whether revenue multiples keep expanding, which is where he turns sceptical of a US$62 billion bull case.
why: A compact explanation of what actually props up top franchise valuations and where the maths gets shaky.
key_points: Doubling revenue in a decade needs only about 7.2% annual growth.
Scarcity and wealth preservation, not upside, drive ultra-wealthy buyers.
A 15-year depreciation tax shield adds to the buyer's return.
Revenue multiples have climbed from roughly 3x to 9x to nearly 20x; whether that keeps going decides the bull case.

application: Useful for any rights holder weighing betting, broadcast and second-screen partners ahead of Australia's 2027 gambling ad rules.
limitations: A hypothetical deal; the author built a second-screen betting product (STADIUUM) and says so.
title: Tabcorp Buys Foxtel Media: Wouldn't That Be a Nice Headline?
role: Writes The Black Book; former head of Australasia for Bleacher Report/TNT Sports, interim media and communications manager for SANZAAR and CMO of BLK Sport
summary: Mortimer plays out the AFR-reported talks in which Tabcorp CEO Gillon McLachlan asked DAZN about buying Foxtel, which DAZN bought for A$3.4 billion in April 2025 and says is not for sale. He sets Tabcorp's roughly A$2 billion equity and A$2.63 billion FY26 revenue against Foxtel's AFL (A$4.5 billion deal to 2031) and NRL (about A$520 million a year) rights, and ties the logic to the 2027 ban on gambling ads during live sport. The US record (Penn's roughly US$4 billion on theScore, Barstool and ESPN Bet), News Corp's quick exit from betr and Sky selling Sky Bet suggest partnership, like ESPN and DraftKings, captures most of the value without ownership.
why: A clear-eyed look at whether owning the broadcast screen is worth it for a betting company, and why commercial partnerships usually beat ownership.

title: The Pitch [#09]: Could Cricket Be Better Packaged as a Tourism Product?
role: Managing Director, TPF Labs, The Players Fund; Sports Pundit
summary: Andy Marston and cricket business consultant and Wisden board member Edward Fitzgibbon argue that cricket's biggest events already work as multi-destination travel products (Ashes tours linking Adelaide, Melbourne, Brisbane and Sydney), but the hotel nights, restaurants and activities fans spend on never show up in the sport's accounts beyond the ticket, per the episode notes.
why: Frames spend around an event as revenue the rights holder is not yet capturing.
key_points: Fans already build whole itineraries around a day or two at the cricket, which the sport could package properly with travel partners, including a personalised itinerary app.
Global expansion (World Cups in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, venues in Japan and China, talk of a German World Cup) works best when new audiences can see the sport in person.
Cricket media covers selection dilemmas but not the business; translating crore into pounds or dollars would make Indian cricket money stories land.
Alt streams for the cricket-curious and UFC Ultimate Fighter style reality formats, starting with associate nations, are suggested growth levers.

application: IP owners in sport and entertainment can ask which creator platforms let them control how their IP looks and who can publish with it before licensing to user-made games.
limitations: The view of a Meta executive promoting his own product; no usage or revenue numbers.
title: Can you build a legitimate video game business on prompts? Meta thinks so
role: Leads The Game Business; previously nine years at MCV and over eight years as head of GamesIndustry.biz
summary: Dring interviews Saxs Persson, VP of Horizon at Meta, about Horizon Studio and Horizon Create, AI tools that let people build games from text prompts and publish them to Instagram and Facebook feeds. Persson argues prompt-built games are a real business for indie teams but not yet for triple-A studios, and that Meta's edge over Roblox and Minecraft is having no fixed art style, so IP owners can represent their properties accurately. He names IP protection and age safety as the conditions for platform trust, noting Dring found an unofficial Pokemon game on another AI platform.
why: A platform owner's case for prompt-built, feed-distributed interactive content, including where it stops being a business and what trust conditions it depends on.

application: Rights holders with research or performance assets can pitch partners on a product development cycle and a named translation team, not just exposure.
limitations: Contract value is undisclosed beyond 'millions'; partnership outcomes are years away.
title: Behind The Scenes At Asics’ New Sport Innovation Center At University Of Michigan
role: Sports and business journalist, Sprungstack; formerly Boardroom, Forbes, Awful Announcing
summary: Sprung reports from the launch of the ASICS Michigan Sport Innovation Center, the brand's first North American R&D lab, staffed by six University of Michigan departments under a five-year, multi-million dollar contract Michigan won after an RFP of more than a year. ASICS North America COO Mike Dougherty says Michigan won because it had a business development team that could fit academic research to ASICS's product cycle; the target is prototypes on elite runners at LA 2028, with Nike and Jordan keeping the athletics apparel deal. The same issue notes the NBA naming Kalshi and Polymarket as preferred prediction market exchanges, with Sportradar as data provider and an MOU with the CFTC.
why: Shows a brand-university partnership built around R&D and product timelines rather than logos, and why the winning bid was about commercial translation.

application: Rights holders planning a new format can compare their model with these launches: broadcast partner, presenting partner, grassroots pathway and investor exit.
limitations: Mostly a descriptive round-up of announcements with little performance data yet.
title: The emergence of new sports competitions
role: Founder, Notice
summary: Hughes maps the wave of new and revamped competitions in Australian sport: Swimming Australia and Nine's team-based Swim GP, the Surfing Super League (launching summer 2028 with a Foxtel deal, built to sell to private investors after four years, against 6.3 million active surfers and a $2.71 billion surf economy), the AO 1 Point Slam grassroots-to-Rod Laver format, Tennis Victoria's State v State Premier League and the NBL Ignite Cup (prize pool up to $550,000 with 7-Eleven as presenting partner). He concludes that success depends on turning initial interest into lasting value for fans, athletes and partners.
why: A useful map of who is launching what format in Australia, with the commercial model behind several of them.

application: Clubs weighing a new or shared venue can list each revenue line they would control as owner versus tenant before crediting design choices, and set before-and-after measures (queue times, dwell time, repeat attendance) for every feature.
limitations: Revenue and valuation figures are Forbes estimates; the piece is a design perspective and does not model returns.
title: Designing stadiums for women: what actually creates value?
role: Founder and editor, Stadium Tech Report
summary: Architect Eleni Kalapoda asks which parts of the Kansas City Current's CPKC Stadium success actually travel. The Longs bought the franchise for about $5 million, built a roughly $140 million, 11,500-seat stadium, and Forbes put 2024 revenue at $36 million (nearly four times the NWSL median) and the club's 2025 value at $275 million, but she argues much of that came from owning and controlling the asset (naming rights, premium, sponsorship inventory, calendar) and the $1 billion Current Landing district, not from women-specific design. Denver Summit is copying the control while designing gender-neutral, San Diego Wave shows the cost of being a tenant, and the Golden State Valkyries sold out every game in an existing arena (averaging 18,064 in 2026).
why: A clear framework for separating what a venue's design earns from what ownership and control of the building earns, with real numbers from four women's clubs.

application: Rights holders pitching growth markets can pair audience reach with a measured base of active participants or known fans before setting sponsor and product targets.
limitations: India-specific data and KPMG figures as reported; the Bayern and ISL items are shorter news-led sections.
title: India can price sport. It can’t count its players.
role: Founder, The State of Play; The Left Field
summary: Ananth's lead argument is that India can value its sport to the crore but cannot say how many people actually play: KPMG puts the market at Rs 1.99 lakh crore for FY26 and sponsorship passed Rs 18,525 crore in 2024, yet there is no consistent national participation measure and the sports ministry counts centres opened, not usage. Brands selling shoes, kit and turf bookings are sizing a market without knowing their customer count. The same edition covers Bayern selling its last allowable 6.7% stake to sponsor Viessmann for a reported 250 million euros (a 3.7 billion euro valuation, members at the 70% floor) and 13 ISL clubs getting a season on free YouTube in 124 days, with 65 million views in five games but sponsors arriving late.
why: A sharp reminder that audience numbers are not customer numbers: commercial plans built on viewership without participation or first-party data are guesses.

application: Rights holders can weigh reach, findability and fan experience alongside fee when choosing distribution partners.
limitations: Summary based on public excerpt; his detailed fixes for each of the four problems are paywalled, and he flags Nielsen data with caution.
title: THE TELEVISION WILL BE ENSHITTIFIED
role: Media cartographer; Media War & Peace; co-host The Media Odyssey; former network executive
summary: Shapiro argues TV is losing audiences because of its own choices, not because social video is cheap. Citing Nielsen directionally, YouTube took a record 15.8% of US TV usage in August 2026, 70% more than Disney and over twice Netflix, and it has out-reached the BBC in the UK for three quarters running. He points to Kantar data that most consumers think YouTube, TikTok and Instagram offer better, more personalised experiences, and blames rising ad loads, price rises, password crackdowns, poor discovery and sport spread across too many platforms.
why: Fragmenting live sport across platforms and loading it with ads is now cited as part of why audiences are leaving TV.

application: Use reach channels for discovery but measure success by fans moved into owned, smaller and higher-value relationships.
limitations: Written about publishing, social media and software, not sport; the sport application is Front Row's, not the author's.

bridge.insight: Thompson: when distribution is free and content is infinite, sustainable value comes from going small, through paid niches and private high-trust groups.
bridge.decision: A club, league or venue digital and membership lead deciding how much to invest in public social reach versus owned memberships, private fan communities and direct channels.
bridge.adaptation: Fans already belong to tribes, so sport starts with a ready-made association; what does not transfer is the solo-creator economics, since clubs must also serve casual fans and sponsors who want scale.
bridge.test: Run one private, member-only community or group channel for a season and compare renewal, spend and data capture with public-social followers. It fails if engagement stays with public platforms and members do not renew at a higher rate.

title: The End of the Internet
role: Author, Stratechery (business and strategy of technology and media)
summary: Thompson argues that each phase of the open internet ended the same way: open access meant infinite competition, which is terrible for business. Ad-funded blogging lost to Google, which captured discovery once distribution was free; the durable model became subscriptions to a niche, making more from customers who really care. Public social media turned into engagement-tuned entertainment while real social networking moved into high-trust group chats. With AI now exposing software flaws at scale and consuming content without returning traffic, he expects the public internet to become a battle zone, and value to move to smaller, private groups and associations: many local markets rather than one global one.
why: A clear case for building smaller, owned, high-trust fan relationships instead of chasing reach on platforms that keep the audience.

application: Commercial teams at clubs outside the elite can use it to argue for recurring, non-competition revenue that cushions bad seasons.
limitations: Summary based on the public excerpt and the author's own X thread; the full review is for paid or claimed readers.
title: Feyenoord Finances 2025/26
role: Anonymous football finance analyst
summary: Swiss Ramble's review of Feyenoord's 2025/26 accounts shows a swing from a 31.1 million euro pre-tax profit to a 17.0 million euro loss. Revenue fell by nearly a third, from 166.7 million to 115.2 million euros, mainly from playing in the Europa League rather than the Champions League, while costs held flat, so the operating loss widened to 78.9 million euros. Player sales profit of 62.6 million euros softened the hit, and his accompanying thread notes 210 million euros of player trading profit over four years, ten times the previous four.
why: A clean example of how dependent mid-sized European clubs are on Champions League money and player trading.

application: Treat live rights, scarcity and direct fan relationships as the defensible assets, and plan monetisation around complements such as tickets, memberships and commerce.
limitations: Summary based on the public tl;dr; the full argument and evidence sit behind the paywall, and part two (implications) is still to come.
title: The Predictable Economic Consequences of Infinite Content
role: The Mediator; former EVP and Chief Strategy Officer, Turner, 2015 to 2018 (verified)
summary: In part one of a two-part series, Shapiro argues that media companies do not need to know how AI will evolve to predict its economic effects. Two things are near certain: consumer attention is not growing and generative AI will sharply cut creation costs. From that he derives a chain of consequences: quality content supply explodes, even good content becomes more substitutable, hit rates fall, creators take share, pricing power weakens, and monetisation shifts to complementary products. Value moves to whoever creates differentiated demand, controls the moment of consumer choice, or monetises complements, and the biggest open question is who controls coordination.
why: If content becomes abundant, rights holders win by owning demand and the fan relationship, not by producing more content.

application: Marketing and partnership teams can set simple rules for when to join a cultural moment, using audience data to decide, and track whether new casual fans stick around.
limitations: A short opinion post built on examples rather than measured results; no data on whether the traffic turned into revenue.
title: Coke, Novig And Engagement Humping…
role: Sports marketing and communications strategist; Columbia University lecturer
summary: Favorito uses Powerade's quick response to the buzz around Sydney Sweeney's Novig campaign to name a tactic he calls Cultural Conversation Relevance: brands, leagues and outlets such as ESPN, CNN and NFL.com reading their audience data and inserting themselves into a cultural moment to reach casual fans they do not normally serve. He points to the Boston Red Sox, whose most valued recent giveaway was a Barbie-themed shirt with nothing to do with baseball, and to a Montclair State study that found the Swift-Kelce crossover chatter was largely benign. His caution is that the play must widen the audience without driving off the core.
why: A practical frame for when a rights holder or sponsor should jump on a cultural moment to reach casual fans, and the risk of alienating the core.

title: How F1 Sponsors Make Brand Activations Feel Earned
role: Writes The Commercial Table, interviews and breakdowns for commercial and marketing teams at rights holders, brands and suppliers in sport
summary: Rob Statham and Jake Smith, who have produced live brand experiences in F1 and now run the agency NINETHREE, explain why many F1 activations fail. Show cars no longer stop people, brands often spend the first year of a three-year deal 'lost at sea' while newer partners make noise, and a simulator can hurt the brands beside it. Their test: take the logo off and ask whether the activation still says anything about the sponsor.
why: A simple test for whether a partnership activation earns its place, usable in any sport or event.

title: The Brewers swapped 1,600 outfield seats for office space, then made the World Series
role: Founder, Huddle Up newsletter; sports business writer and investor
summary: Pompliano points out that the Milwaukee Brewers removed 1,600 outfield seats last year to build offices for their baseball operations staff. At about $1,000 a ticket, he estimates those seats would have brought in $1.6 million per World Series home game, or $6.4 million if Milwaukee hosts four. He calls it not a huge deal, but bad timing for a project that was only just finished.
why: A simple reminder that seat inventory is revenue capacity, and that venue changes made for the off season can cost the most at peak demand.

title: 🔵 “Fuel a life, don’t fill a feed”
role: Founder and MD, Motive Unknown (music marketing agency, UK); Network Notes
summary: Hemmings uses Pinterest search data (40% of Gen Z wish social media had never been invented; 63% intentionally unplug) to argue marketing must change. Borrowing Pinterest's lines 'design the exit' and 'be a bridge to something real', he says music marketing should move fans from scrolling into creative, engaging experiences.
why: Supports interactive, purposeful fan experiences over feed-filling content.

title: Tiptoeing on the Podcast: Who Owns the Meme? D.C.’s Resale Cap Goes to Court & the Brewers’ Timeless Ticket Fumble
role: Senior Director, Live Music and Touring, Billboard; founder Decibel
summary: Dave Brooks and entertainment attorney Michael Seville work through three live-business legal fights: the resellers' court challenge to Washington DC's 110% resale price cap, the Milwaukee Brewers' 'Timeless Tickets' backlash on the eve of the World Series, and who profits when an AI-fuelled meme goes viral.
why: Resale price caps are spreading, and the Brewers case shows how a lifetime ticket product turns into a loyalty liability when demand spikes.
key_points: DC's RESALE Act, in force from 1 January, caps concert and theatre resale at 110% of face value, fees included. The resellers' suit leaves all-in pricing, the speculative ticket ban and the $25,000 bond alone and attacks only the cap, on six counts.
Seville explains why long-shot claims get added to open up discovery, and notes similar caps in the UK and Ontario have not produced the collapse resellers predicted.

In 2015 the Brewers sold 1,000 'Timeless Tickets' at $1,000, good for any future home game. With World Series get-in prices about $2,600, holders were offered standing room; the club has admitted a mistake and offered a fix.
The hosts' read: 'subject to availability' fine print does not protect goodwill, and the club left a PR win on the table.
On the meme: purely AI-generated footage cannot be copyrighted in the US, so the artist's upside comes through streaming and label licensing deals with TikTok and YouTube.

title: How G2 Could Unlock One of Esports Marketing's Biggest Untapped Opportunities
role: Esports and gaming marketing agency founder; lecturer; 20+ years in esports
summary: Decker argues the big esports question is how to monetise reach beyond sponsors' goods. G2 and Tencent Games are running a PUBG Mobile amateur tournament on a custom map inspired by Counter-Strike's Dust II, via G2's in-house agency 62. He sees teams turning fanbases into player acquisition channels for publishers.
why: A model for rights holders selling fan action (sign-ups, installs) to partners, not just impressions.

title: Why shouldn’t the NWSL aim for 30 teams?
role: Editor, The Boston Globe; author, The Fixture
summary: NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman keeps saying the league should reach 30 teams like the men's leagues, and McInerney agrees. The league added Boston and Denver this year, adds Atlanta and Columbus in 2028, and will start the process for teams 19 and 20. She predicts where it might expand.
why: Expansion means new clubs building fan bases and partner programmes from scratch.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Independent Football Regulator CEO Richard Monks explains the new levy on clubs
role: Lecturer, University of Liverpool; The Price of Football
summary: Kieran Maguire presses Independent Football Regulator CEO Richard Monks on the levy that will fund the IFR from 2027/28 and on how hard it will come down on owners, debt and loss-making clubs. Monks sets out a budget of about 20m pounds a year charged in proportion across the 116 regulated clubs, and insists the regulator will stay independent of government.
why: Regulation is becoming a fixed cost of running an English club, and owner tests, liquidity rules and a possible imposed distribution deal will shape club budgets and valuations.
key_points: The levy is about 20.3m pounds a year: 18.3m operating costs, a 1m litigation reserve and 1m a year recovering government set-up costs over 10 years (per the IFR's release that day).

Charges scale by league, European competition and commercial income over 150m pounds. Most clubs pay about 0.1% of revenue and none more than 0.5%; most Premier League clubs about 600,000 pounds, League Two clubs about 6,000.

Per a published transcript summary, the State of the Game report found 94% of clubs loss-making, and the IFR will run a risk-based model with about 100 staff, each supervisor covering about seven clubs.
Monks says the IFR has powers over owners, debt and liquidity, and will use its backstop if the Premier League and EFL cannot agree distributions and parachute payments.
His warning to badly run clubs: 'we'll be with you every week'.

title: Amazon's Big Bets on Music, Twitch, and Podcasts
role: Founder, Trapital
summary: Dan Runcie's Trapital Summit session with Steve Boom, Amazon's VP of Audio, Twitch and Games, on the competition for attention. Per Runcie's published takeaways, Boom argues against exclusive podcast deals, says Amazon Music is still growing, and explains why streaming prices will rise only slowly.
why: A major platform's view on exclusivity, pricing and direct fan payments, all live questions for any rights holder building its own subscription or creator content.
key_points: Amazon avoids podcast exclusivity because creators need broad distribution; it earns through ads and ecosystem perks instead.
Amazon Music's free and paid tiers are both growing, though paid growth has slowed in developed markets; the paid tier only launched in India in June 2026.
Music streaming is undervalued, but raising prices fast risks churn given free ad-supported options and subscription fatigue.
Twitch has moved beyond gaming into major sports events, and most of its revenue comes from viewers paying streamers directly, not ads.
Audio's edge in the attention war is that it does not need your full attention.

title: UP577 Spin Class: The Premier League, Man City and the battle over the story
role: Owner and editor, Unofficial Partner
summary: With the Premier League having 'won the facts' (Manchester City found guilty of 114 of 115 charges, with 830m pounds of revenue inflated through sham sponsorships, per the episode notes), former Premier League comms director Dan Johnson and Nick Harris of Sporting Intelligence argue the fight is now over the story. They pull apart City's comms playbook and the League's silence.
why: Sham sponsorship findings put related-party deals and disclosure under the spotlight, which affects how every rights holder prices and reports its partnerships.
key_points: The League's long silence left a vacuum that City's network of former players, ambassadors and friendly voices filled.
Pundits who act as a 'third-party endorser network' should declare who pays them.
The political thread: Andy Burnham's interview, Number 10's clean-up, the 14 September Downing Street meeting, and whether City was ever a private investment rather than a state project.
What the sanction should be, and whether punishing the champions damages or strengthens the Premier League product.

title: How to Fill a Soccer Stadium: Ticketing & Fan Growth with Jim McCarthy
role: Football business journalist; The Soccer Business newsletter and podcast
summary: Jim McCarthy, founder of the Gold Star live event marketplace (12 million buyers) and now at Impresario, argues clubs are burning fan trust with revenue-maximising ticketing and should manage for full seats and the whole matchday instead. Per the episode notes, he and Simon Evans use FIFA's World Cup pricing as the cautionary case and set out how an MLS or USL club should grow its crowd.
why: A practical playbook for turning one-off demand into repeat attendance and owned buyer data, with no-show rates and revenue per seat as the measures to watch.
key_points: FIFA ran the World Cup as a revenue-maximising event, and that has a cost in fan trust (per the notes).
Season ticket no-shows of 20% or more are common; rewarding attendance works better than penalising absence.
Revenue per seat matters more than average ticket price, and the episode tests whether cheaper tickets lift in-stadium spend.
When a star like Messi comes to town, clubs should act on the buyer data, not just enjoy a one-off sell-out.
Gen Z's appetite for real-world events is a growth opening for soccer as matchday expectations rise.

title: Horizontal Multi-Club Ownership: Building Value Beyond Promotion
role: Founder, Berkida Ventures; The Berkida Brief
summary: With David Dwinger of Estrella Football Group, the brief explains horizontal multi-club ownership: a network where each club keeps its identity and local management while the group shares systems, specialist support and commercial relationships. It includes an Australian club portfolio.
why: Shared group capability is where centralised fan and partner tools get bought.

title: How Messi brings new fans to MLS – Chris Schlosser
role: Founder, Sports Geek
summary: A Sports Geek throwback (originally episode 368) with MLS's Chris Schlosser. In the published transcript excerpt he says MLS was already having a record year before Messi arrived, but Messi's global following beat expectations on social views and Apple viewership, and the job is to use him as an entry point to the rest of the league.
why: A star-driven audience spike only pays off if the league converts new fans into lasting relationships. A re-run, not new.
key_points: Innovation programmes need dedicated resources and clear success metrics.
Testing in youth leagues and lower divisions speeds up product validation.
Fan engagement tech should improve access and convenience, not distract from the live sport.
Star signings (Beckham then, Messi now) pay off when fans who come for the star move on to other teams, stadiums and stories.

title: Mark Walter Says There Are No Victims. Retirees Disagree.
role: Founder, Huddle Up newsletter; sports business writer and investor
summary: Dodgers owner Mark Walter faces lawsuits alleging he misled investors. Pompliano explains the allegation that annuity money from Walter's insurance companies was routed to buy teams including the Dodgers, Lakers and Chelsea, and Walter's defence.
why: Ownership finance risk at some of the biggest clubs.

title: The difficult questions; Rugby is a problem magnet; Declare your interests; Should pundits say who’s paying them; Tottenham’s big ideas man; The T20 misread
role: Owner and editor, Unofficial Partner
summary: Gillis's weekly Unofficial Partner newsletter: the difficult questions, rugby as a 'problem magnet', declaring interests, and pundits. Only the subscribe line is in the feed, so open it for detail.
why: Weekly commentary on sport's commercial and media issues.

title: The key to unlocking fandom begins with these fan archetypes
role: Managing Director, MIDiA Research
summary: MIDiA argues fandom is not one-size-fits-all but a mix of engagement types and activity levels. The post builds on the four core fan archetypes from last year's Defining entertainment superfans report. The full post is for MIDiA clients; only the teaser is public.
why: A segmentation lens for fan programmes: different archetypes need different engagement mechanics, not one superfan tier.

title: Where now for Mass Effect? Plus, Ken Kutaragi’s console fears and the rise of Poki
role: Leads The Game Business; previously nine years at MCV and over eight years as head of GamesIndustry.biz
summary: Dring reads EA's closure of BioWare as part of a wider industry focus on big bets. BioWare was 12.5% of EA's cuts, which aim to save $700 million, and about 50 people were on the cancelled Mass Effect project. Publishers including EA, Microsoft, Sony and Take-Two are concentrating on their largest franchises. He suggests licensing dormant brands such as Mass Effect or Dead Space to independent veteran teams, as this year's Star Wars games showed can work on tight budgets.
why: Shows the portfolio logic squeezing mid-size IP, and a licensing model rights holders in any entertainment business could borrow.
key_points: EA will run fewer simultaneous large projects and paused a Sims project and cut Skate.
Single-player RPGs cost a lot with comparatively low upside for a company of EA's margins.
Ken Kutaragi tells Dring there is a 'very real danger' the console era is ending.

title: How DAZN Is Taking Over Local Pro Sports Media Rights
role: Sports and business journalist, Sprungstack; formerly Boardroom, Forbes, Awful Announcing
summary: After Diamond Sports' bankruptcy left NBA, NHL and MLB teams without local TV homes, DAZN took full local streaming rights or partnerships with 11 NBA and 6 NHL teams, often paying less than before and sometimes on revenue share. DAZN's Pete Oliver says the cable RSN model 'collapsed' and pitches an affordable season pass instead (Cavs: $20 a month or $120 a season), with 15+ more local packages planned and a possible bid for the NBA's local streaming hub in 2027 or 2028. The post also covers Jalen Hurts fallout and NFL private equity.
why: Local rights moving to a streamer changes who owns the direct fan relationship and data for those teams.

title: If the noise around the WNBA Finals seems quiet, this might be why
role: Editor, The Boston Globe; author, The Fixture
summary: McInerney notes the WNBA Finals have been strong (a sold-out 17,099 for Game 3 in Atlanta) but CBS's Jack Maloney reported no media access between Games 1 and 2. She argues the league's access policy matters if it wants the Finals covered.
why: Coverage access shapes how much storytelling fans get between games.

title: RTL & YOUTUBE: REDEFINING BROADCAST
role: Media cartographer; Media War & Peace; co-host The Media Odyssey; former network executive
summary: Evan Shapiro's MIPCOM keynote with RTL Deutschland CEO Stephan Schmitter and YouTube EMEA head Pedro Pina on their 'partnership of equals'. Shapiro's write-up argues RTL disproves the cannibalisation myth: YouTube has become an extension of its broadcast flywheel rather than a threat.
why: Evidence that putting live sport and content on YouTube can grow subscriptions and ad revenue instead of cannibalising them.
key_points: RTL had no YouTube relationship 36 months ago; it now puts library content, live news and live sports there.
It packages ad sales across YouTube and its own platforms, and uses YouTube to drive subscriptions to RTL+ and Sky Deutschland.
RTL found new, younger and more male audiences on YouTube and grew platform revenues by 492%, per Shapiro.
The session covers the theory (Pina's 'new golden age of television') and how RTL runs it day to day for viewing, subscriptions and ad sales.

title: The Geography of Sports Innovation
role: Founder and GP, Profluence (Profluence Capital)
summary: Petcash argues sports innovation clusters geographically because it needs athletes, facilities, manufacturers and obsessed communities, not just software. Examples include California for golf and Portland for running and outdoor (Nike, Columbia, Keen, Adidas North America). He looks at which hubs are next.
why: Useful for thinking about where sports tech partners and buyers concentrate.

title: Decoding Nike’s Subtle Investor Relations Rebrand
role: Founder and writer, Sportsverse; award-winning business journalist
summary: Nike's investor relations page has swapped 'Nike Inc. is a Growth Company' for 'NIKE IS A SPORT COMPANY'. Miller argues the shift signals the brand letting go of beliefs that no longer ring true. Most of the piece is paywalled.
why: Brand positioning signal ahead of Nike's 16 to 17 Nov Investor Day.

byline: Evan Shapiro and Marion Ranchet (The Media Odyssey)
title: WHY BROADCASTERS ARE PARTNERING WITH THE PLATFORM THEY ONCE FEARED
role: Media cartographer; Media War & Peace; co-host The Media Odyssey; former network executive
summary: YouTube EMEA's Pedro Pina and RTL Deutschland CEO Stephan Schmitter explain how RTL went from no YouTube relationship three years ago to treating it as a partner. RTL put about 200 full episodes of the worn-out 1996 series Cobra 11 on YouTube, earning about 30 million views in a year from a mostly male, 30-ish audience, and saw 123% more first video views and about 26% more subscriptions on RTL+. RTL's Ad Alliance now sells RTL+, RTL, Sky and YouTube inventory as one package, which Schmitter says brings near double-digit millions of incremental revenue, with a path agreed through 2030.
why: A measured case for putting old archive on social platforms to drive owned subscriptions, relevant to any rights holder with a back catalogue.
key_points: The cannibalisation fear did not hold: catalogue on YouTube worked as a subscription funnel one click away on the TV screen.
Partners that sell YouTube inventory with their own sales force get higher CPMs, especially on the big screen.
YouTube creators supply pre-shows and highlights RTL cannot make itself, and gain credibility by appearing on RTL shows.
Linear and free-to-air remain a big part of the business; YouTube is one channel, not the answer.

title: How Tampa Bay Rebuilt Its Brand After Tom Brady Copy title
role: Sports business commentator and brand strategist; host, Moneyball: The Business of Sport
summary: Tampa Bay Buccaneers creative director Dan Beltran explains how the club rebuilt its visual identity after Tom Brady's retirement. Rather than starting with a logo, font or design trend, his team photographed thousands of images across Tampa and drew on the city's Cuban and Spanish heritage, historic architecture and cigar industry, so the identity belongs to the place rather than any one star. Keenan and Beltran also discuss how player brands and club brands relate, and why clubs need to understand their fans before deciding what content should look like.
why: A practical approach to brand work for any club facing life after a defining player.
key_points: A sporting identity built around one superstar has to be rebuilt when he leaves; one built on the city lasts longer.
Know the fans first, then decide the content style.
Clubs can evolve their look without losing what supporters see as theirs, with Newcastle Knights and NZ Warriors as local comparisons.

title: The Business of Building Everything
role: Writes Per Cap on the economics of themed entertainment; 12+ years in investment banking, private credit and corporate development
summary: Using Saudi Arabia's Aquarabia water park as the opening case, Vo examines Falcon's Beyond's strategy of owning design, ride systems, IP and destinations. In a worked example, winning $18M of a $50M attraction instead of a $3M design contract lifts revenue sixfold but adds only about $300,000 of profit, which a 5% overrun on direct costs would wipe out, while the work can need $3M of peak funding. He compares other integrators (WhiteWater, MACK with Europa-Park, Sansei with FORREC, TAIT with Thinkwell) and argues that where a company starts decides which risks it takes on.
why: A clear framework for when owning more of the delivery chain pays, relevant to venue, production and events suppliers.

title: How American Express's NFL Partnership Is Built Around Membership
role: Founder and publisher, Faze 3 Sport; Culture of Sport and Original Football
summary: Skilling interviews Shiz Suzuki, American Express's VP of global brand sponsorships, after an NFL London game at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Her framing is that Amex is 'in the business of membership', so its NFL, F1 and Brighton deals are designed as access benefits for card members: hospitality, presales, priority merchandise access with Fanatics, and commentary radios that help first-time NFL fans follow the game. Amex treats sponsorships as 'business driver levers', measured on awareness, consideration, acquisition and retention.
why: Shows a sponsor buying rights to make its own membership more valuable, which changes what rights holders should package and how they should prove the deal works.

title: Checking in on the professional women’s volleyball wars
role: Editor, The Boston Globe; author, The Fixture
summary: Two US women's pro volleyball leagues are expanding at once with opposite models. Major League Volleyball (12 teams in 2027) has local owners, a draft and free agency, and LA Times owner Patrick Soon-Shiong reportedly paid $15 to $20 million for a team. LOVB Pro is vertically integrated from youth clubs and launched league-owned; it is now bringing in celebrity investor groups and has hired the search firm the NWSL used to find owners. Both appointed new commissioners (from the NFL via USA Volleyball, and from Nike's Jordan brand) and are building towards LA 2028.
why: A rare side-by-side of league-owned and team-owned models competing for the same players and fans.

title: 186 - 2026 MiLB Business Summit Recap: What's Working, What's Changing, and What's Next
role: Host, Sports Marketing Machine podcast; 21+ years in sports marketing
summary: Neisser, Sam Goldfeder and Andy Milovich recap the MiLB Business Summit in Louisville. Minor league teams are moving from viral-for-its-own-sake promotions to repeatable campaigns tied to local identity, such as the Albuquerque Isotopes' Native American Heritage Night. Ownership groups now expect clearer ROI, so teams are asking about the incremental lift of staples like Friday fireworks. Data is replacing 'spray and pray' email and promotions.
why: A snapshot of how the most promotion-driven corner of sport is becoming data- and ROI-led.
key_points: Teams are balancing premium experiences against affordability with value-added tickets, theme nights and offers like $5 Tuesdays.
AI is drawing interest as a way to raise output without adding headcount, including helping fans picture suite parties or sponsor activations.
Predictive models and weather forecasts are being used to time offers, alongside better channel attribution.
Community presence and storytelling remain the base that technology should support, not replace.

title: Why Esports Has Too Many Teams and Why Most of Them Fail
role: Esports and gaming marketing agency founder; lecturer; 20+ years in esports
summary: Drawing on 20 years in esports, Decker argues the ecosystem cannot support as many teams as traditional sport because, being mostly online, small teams lack a natural niche such as a home region that delivers loyal fans and local sponsors. The few niches that exist are a smaller country (as ENCE did in Finland), a cheaper, less popular game, or unusual branding. Most small teams instead become budget copies of G2 or Team Liquid, which neither fans nor sponsors value.
why: A clear case that without geography, a property must find another reason for fans and sponsors to choose it.

title: What the 2026 WNBA attendance trends say about the future
role: Editor, The Boston Globe; author, The Fixture
summary: The 2026 WNBA season had 212 sellouts (64% of games, a record) and average attendance up almost 5%. From 2027, 11 of 15 teams will play in NBA or NHL arenas, and in Sportico's valuations the four lowest-revenue teams were those outside professional venues. McInerney argues the constraint is now ticket pricing and front-office capacity, not venues: when a scarce ticket becomes commonplace in an 18,000-seat arena, sales and community staff must grow. She singles out the Washington Mystics, stuck in a 4,200-seat facility under contract to 2037, as the outlier.
why: A useful read on what moving into bigger arenas changes for a team's ticketing and community operations.

title: The NBA Is More Reliant On TikTok Creators Than Ever Before
role: Sports and business journalist, Sprungstack; formerly Boardroom, Forbes, Awful Announcing
summary: Sprung reports from the NBA's briefing on its 2026-27 digital plans. Last season 210 million people in the US watched an NBA game, and league content drew 430 billion views across platforms. The NBA and TikTok are launching a global program for 500 up-and-coming creators, chosen with Ripple Analytics, who get storylines, IP, highlights and access to tentpole events, with the access itself as the main incentive. Any TikTok post using #NBA automatically gets a 'tap to watch' link to that night's game. 'Tap to watch' is spreading to X, betting, fantasy and editorial sites, alongside an AI stats chatbot in the NBA app.
why: A detailed blueprint for using small creators, not just stars, as a distribution layer that sends viewers to live games.

title: Football's Academy Factories Are Big Business
role: Founder and publisher, Faze 3 Sport; Culture of Sport and Original Football
summary: Skilling explains why academy sales have become core football business. Real Madrid has made over €500 million from academy players since 2005 (per AS), often keeping sell-on shares and buyback options, as with Nico Paz at Como. Chelsea made over £250 million from academy sales in three years and City about £215 million in profit over four seasons. Because academy costs are not capitalised, a homegrown player's sale is almost pure accounting profit, which mattered under PSR and still counts under the Premier League's new Squad Cost Ratio (85% of football revenue plus net trading profit).
why: Explains how youth development doubles as a financing tool under spending rules, and the cost it carries with fans attached to homegrown players.

title: UP576 World Rugby Chief on Private Equity, Disruptor Leagues and Following FIFA in to the US
role: Owner and editor, Unofficial Partner
summary: World Rugby chief executive Alan Gilpin, who spent nine years at IMG selling Rugby World Cup rights, explains a sport financially dependent on one event: the men's World Cup brings in about 85 to 90% of World Rugby's income. He is targeting a surplus of more than $1 billion from the 2031 tournament in the US, even though rugby cannot make FIFA-style demands of NFL stadium owners and staging is far more expensive there. He says France 2023's losses ended the outsourced hosting model, and calls rugby's biggest problem self-inflicted: 'we're competing amongst ourselves'.
why: A candid look at the economics of a governing body that lives or dies by one tournament, and of taking it to the US.
key_points: World Rugby is hiring FIFA's people and running a host-city process modelled on the 2026 football World Cup.
It cannot demand commercially clean venues from NFL owners, so the focus is margin over headline revenue.
Private equity in Premiership Rugby, R360 and LIV-style disruptors, the women's Lions and the streamers' appetite for 'eventised' products are all covered.
He argues digital metrics like RugbyPass clip views can push fans the wrong way up the funnel.

title: The Athlete Is the Creator. The University Is Becoming the Network.
role: Disruptive Play; co-founder Creator Sports Network
summary: Cal has opened a Twitch studio with StreamU for about ten hours a week of athlete-driven programming, with Arkansas, Texas A&M, Baylor and Houston expected to follow. Cohen warns that sports properties often find distribution harder than production. He argues universities should build networks that reach fans where athletes already have audiences, not just another owned channel. He calls for shared economics (national sponsors funding cross-school series, sold through rights partners like Learfield or Playfly), clear answers on who owns the audience when an athlete leaves, and conference-wide networks for scale.
why: A framework for any league or club organising its athletes' creator audiences into a sellable media product.

title: EuroLeague’s answer to the NBA
role: Founder, The State of Play; The Left Field
summary: After its shareholders rejected the NBA's proposed European league, EuroLeague set out a 10-year franchise plan: €3.4bn distributed to clubs (€2.2bn from revenue, €1.2bn from franchise fees) and a projected combined value of €13.38bn for the league and its teams. The NBA says it will still launch a European league with FIBA, targeting 2028, with bids expected from Champions League football club owners. The issue also summarises FIFPRO's report on women's football: average monthly pay has tripled since 2017 to $2,601 (median $1,669), but only 57% say pay covers the cost of playing and only 8 of 30 leagues have collective agreements.
why: Two competing models for the business of European basketball are now on the table, with football club owners in the middle.

title: When premium is the product
role: Founder and editor, Stadium Tech Report
summary: A profile of Intercoastal Motor Car & Yacht Club, a planned 143-acre Atlantic City development combining a 2.44-mile FIA-spec driving course, luxury residences, car storage, restaurants and a museum on the former Bader Field airport. Its premium-experience lead, CTO and CEO are designing the guest journey before the buildings and systems exist. Jessica Gaffney 'sits in the gray' between departments, defining what the property must know about each guest and where a person should take over, and refuses to copy a single luxury benchmark. CTO Tod Caflisch plans local compute for low-latency track safety, multiple carriers, and an underground service tunnel so fiber can be added later without digging up the course.
why: A rare look at designing premium hospitality and venue technology from a blank sheet.
key_points: Drawings are cheap to change now and the building will not be, so experience requirements are being turned into physical requirements early.
Premium customers resist categories: some value access, others recognition, privacy or convenience.
The site needs 2.5 million cubic yards of fill, which also shapes the course and contains noise; geothermal district heating and cooling is planned.
CEO Michael Binder's 'polished floor' test: premium detail extends to the mechanic's workshop, not just the software.

title: Carolina Chiappero [#93]: How Juventus Approaches Innovation Holistically
role: Managing Director, TPF Labs, The Players Fund; Sports Pundit
summary: Juventus innovation manager Carolina Chiappero explains how the club runs innovation as a cross-functional service: she finds internal needs, scouts outside solutions and tests them with internal champions. Its Juventus Forward programme takes a 'squad' of startups through 12-month pilots designed for adoption, now spanning performance, digital marketing, facilities and communications.
why: A practical model for turning a club's startup programme into adopted tools and sponsor activation rather than press-release pilots.
key_points: Innovation is defined as anything that makes the club work better or creates new value, so it sits across departments rather than in one team.
Pilots are built for adoption, not for their own sake, and more departments join with each batch.
The value stacks up: the brand attracts technology at net-zero cost, each pilot targets time savings, cost cuts or new revenue.
The next step is partner-driven innovation, where startups also serve club sponsors and innovation becomes activation.

title: Chiefs v Chiefs, Spurs x Spurs: Litigation or Collaboration?
role: Writes The Black Book; former head of Australasia for Bleacher Report/TNT Sports, interim media and communications manager for SANZAAR and CMO of BLK Sport
summary: Mortimer contrasts two responses to a shared name in the same week. New Zealand Rugby sought an urgent injunction against the NRL's new Papua New Guinea Chiefs, whose name overlaps a Waikato brand trademarked since 1998; on 16 October 2026 Justice Grau declined it because the ARLC undertook not to promote the brand in New Zealand before a 2027 trial. Meanwhile Tottenham Hotspur and the San Antonio Spurs ran a joint hackathon. He argues defensive IP strategy can cost reach and gate revenue, and walks through the trademark tests at issue.
why: A useful lens on when brand protection helps and when it limits growth across codes and markets.

title: Why A Live Nation & Ticketmaster Breakup Could Be Bad For Fans + Legal Challenges to DC's RESALE ACT with GUEST HOST RANDY NICHOLS
role: Senior Director, Live Music and Touring, Billboard; founder Decibel
summary: Dave Brooks and ticketing expert Randy Nichols walk through what happens if a judge forces Live Nation to sell Ticketmaster, with 34 states and DC seeking divestiture and a remedies trial possible from February. They weigh four routes (a spinoff, a $10 to $15 billion private equity buyout, a strategic buyer such as Fanatics or Eventim, or a full carve-up) and agree none is likely to lower fees. They also cover the resale industry's lawsuit against DC's 10%-over-face resale cap and a DOJ BOTS Act case against a broker accused of spending over $1.3 billion on tickets.
why: The most practical guide yet to how a Ticketmaster breakup could change ticketing deals, fees and resale rules for venues and promoters.
key_points: A spinoff or a debt-funded buyout could push service fees up, not down, because the new owner carries the debt.
Randy Nichols makes the case for Fanatics as a buyer, extending Ticketmaster into college sports, merchandise and trading cards; Brooks warns rivals could then face a trillion-dollar company.

The resale lawsuit against DC (backed by SeatGeek, Vivid Seats, Gametime and TickPick) argues reach, profitability and compelled speech; Nichols notes UK disclosure rules and face-value platforms like Tixel already work.
The San Diego broker allegedly beat purchase limits for 83,000 events and made at least $120 million reselling, showing the BOTS Act covers any method of getting round limits, not only bots.

title: NFL 2026 Innovation Review
role: Founder, FutureSport Co; former lead, City Fan Labs (City Football Group)
summary: Farren picks three NFL innovation stories. FAN.live gives Creator Sports Network's 2,000+ creators a live 3D NFL broadcast built from Genius Sports data, so 'one game becomes a thousand broadcasts' outside the TV rights. Sony's Hawk-Eye supported 630 officiating events and 322 replay reviews last season with 360 boundary cameras and virtual line-to-gain measurement. And the NFL, which has pulled fan data from all 32 clubs into one database, is piloting an Adobe AI content tool because campaigns that needed a couple of thousand assets now need hundreds of thousands. His thesis, the 'Post-TV Playbook': capture once, render endless assets for different audiences.
why: Shows how data-rendered broadcasts and automated content let a league reach new audiences without cannibalising TV rights.

limitations: Written about AI software pricing; the venue application is Front Row's, not the author's.

bridge.insight: Made-up currencies and quantity-based tiers ('more usage', bigger credit numbers) hide value; each unit should map to an outcome the customer can picture (Verna, on AI software pricing).
bridge.decision: A festival, venue or club commercial lead setting cashless credit, token or membership tier pricing, and deciding how to show what each unit or tier buys.
bridge.adaptation: Venue costs per item are predictable, unlike AI compute, so the cost-uncertainty half does not transfer. The mental-accounting and unclear-unit half does, and unspent credit draws fan and regulator scrutiny.
bridge.test: At one event, show dollar equivalents next to token prices at some bars or in the app and compare spend per head, top-ups and refund requests. The analogy fails if fans already read tokens as dollars.

title: What on earth is going on with AI pricing and packaging?
role: Growth operator and adviser; writes Elena's Growth Scoop
summary: Verna, who leads growth at Lovable, tours AI pricing pages and finds plans sold as 'more', '5x' or hundreds of millions of tokens without saying what a customer gets. She names four problems: invented currencies (credits and tokens work like casino chips through mental accounting), bigger numbers mistaken for value, no clear unit of consumption, and unpredictable cost per task. She defends credits as a way to bundle tools with different costs, but argues the winner will make the cost of getting something done understandable, predictable and in the customer's control.
why: Cashless credits, tokens and tiered memberships are common at venues and festivals. Her point is that customers need to see what each unit actually buys.

title: The Golden State Valkyries crafted the perfect WNBA expansion blueprint
role: Editor, The Boston Globe; author, The Fixture
summary: McInerney sets out the Golden State Valkyries' expansion playbook as the team reached the WNBA Finals in its second season. Joe Lacob paid $50 million for the franchise in 2023; it is now valued at $850 million to $1 billion, and revenue rose from $78 million in 2025 to $100 million in 2026. President Jess Smith rejected borrowing the Warriors' colours, held off selling sponsorships until the brand was public, and targeted three fan lanes: existing women's sports fans, traditional men's sports fans, and 'bright believers' drawn by community. Every Chase Center game has sold out, season tickets are capped, and only 8% of the 12,000 season-ticket holders also hold Warriors tickets.
why: A concrete model for the new Cleveland, Detroit and Philadelphia owners, who each paid about $250 million: a separate brand, its own staff, and the shared venue used as an asset.

title: ⚽ English Football’s £9bn Question
role: Founder, Berkida Ventures; The Berkida Brief
summary: Marinelli reads the Independent Football Regulator's draft State of the Game report for investors. The top five English tiers earn about £9bn a year, yet an estimated 94% of clubs lost money before tax and over a quarter said they could not survive a month without new owner funding. He argues buyers must fund the whole ownership period, not just the purchase, and plan the equity and debt mix from day one. The Championship's new 85% squad-cost rule could let total spending rise from £1.02bn to £1.48bn, raising the cost of competing. In the IFR's model, clubs that stayed in the Premier League averaged a 13% cumulative return.
why: The clearest investor reading of the regulator's evidence: club values can rise while returns stay thin once the funding needed along the way is counted.

title: The next big thing in games is low tech
role: Co-founder of SuperData Research (acquired by Nielsen); teaches the Business of Video Games at NYU Stern; author of One Up
summary: Van Dreunen challenges the idea that better technology makes better games. AAA budgets have risen about tenfold since 2000 and the biggest spend now goes on user acquisition, while low-tech play is growing: Asmodee reported a record year, Hasbro keeps growing on Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering, and a Kantar study found more than half of people still play board games monthly, with 73% saying it helps them meet people. He warns that AI savings may simply restart the cycle of bigger, costlier games, and that the defensible strategy is giving people a reason to play together.
why: A useful counterweight to tech-first thinking: social, low-cost formats can win attention and spend.

title: Fixing Call of Duty: Inside Activision’s Modern Warfare 4 comeback plan
role: Leads The Game Business; previously nine years at MCV and over eight years as head of GamesIndustry.biz
summary: Dring interviews Activision CMO Tyler Bahl on rebuilding trust in Call of Duty. Last year's Black Ops 7 launched 50% below its predecessor in Europe, finished fifth in the US (the series' lowest since 2008), and Battlefield 6 was 2025's best-selling shooter. Ampere data show monthly players falling from about 40 million in 2024 to the mid-20 millions in 2026. Bahl says Modern Warfare 4 is judged on whether fans care, not a sales target.
why: A rare on-record account of how a mega-franchise responds to fan fatigue: product changes, community access and nostalgia.
key_points: Activision is ending back-to-back sub-franchise sequels; a future title starts a new sub-franchise.
Surprise PlayStation ports of Black Ops 1 and 2 pushed players back towards 40 million and are shaping future games.
Rebuilding trust meant showing the game at more than 20 events, including four booths at Gamescom, and a behind-the-scenes YouTube series.
Much of the franchise's coverage now comes from influencers rather than press.

title: When the math stops mathing: Fandom signals in the agentic AI era
role: Music industry analyst, MIDiA Research
summary: Cirisano argues that personal AI agents such as Instinct will remove the friction (presales, waitlists, queues) that the music industry has long used to tell casual listeners from dedicated fans.
