RAYE recently received 1.8 million presale sign-ups for a 5,000-seat show after agents created hundreds of thousands of fake registrations for ticket brokers. Real fans will increasingly use agents too, so platforms will have to deal with them rather than block them. Big social followings already fail to predict ticket sales, and MIDiA data shows music playing a shrinking role in younger people's identities even as streaming grows. She proposes measuring relationships over time instead: outcomes like attending multiple concerts, IRL interactions, and deliberate friction.
why: A warning for any ticketing or fan-data strategy built on effort-based signals such as presale sign-ups.

title: A Conversation With Ari Emanuel About Entertainment and AI
role: Author, Stratechery (business and strategy of technology and media)
summary: Ben Thompson and Ari Emanuel, executive chair of WME and TKO (UFC and WWE) and founder of the live events company MARI, discuss entertainment after AI. They agree that if AI does everything digital better, in-person experiences that cannot be disintermediated gain value. Emanuel calls MARI a pro-AI bet, not an anti-AI one, and expects its multiples to rise. He explains TKO's system for monetising events: a model started at UFC and taken to WWE, combining sponsorship, site fees from host cities, premium ticketing and broadcast deals. MARI now applies it to acquired events such as Frieze art fairs and Collect-A-Con, expanding them to new cities including Abu Dhabi.
why: A leading live-events operator explains why AI makes in-person events more valuable, and the repeatable commercial system TKO uses to monetise them.
key_points: Emanuel says broadcast partners are all moving to subscription-plus-ads models, and sport is one of the biggest drivers of the ad tier.
Thompson argues AI agents threaten search ad models once the human is out of the loop, while live events and 'the generation of human desire' gain value.
Emanuel expects AI to mean more content and new creators, but still sees great creative talent as scarce.

title: The Kogan Window; The argument for short term thinking; Doing things vs Talking about doing things; Never Raine’s; Latin for the Judging; That’s so AI; That samey feeling
role: Owner and editor, Unofficial Partner
summary: After the Independent Football Regulator's first State of the Game report, Gillis argues chair David Kogan, on a fixed term to May 2030 with no electorate, should act as if he has about a year of political capital. He sets out the regulator's dated roadmap: the levy consultation now, the Championship's Squad Cost Ratio in 2026/27, government funding ending and the levy falling on the 116 clubs in 2027/28, three stress tests per club due in May 2028 (in the final season of current media deals), and full licences in May 2030, the month Kogan's term ends.
why: A one-page timeline of when English football's financial regulation actually bites, and why the first year matters most.

title: FINDING YOUR AUDIENCE FROM THE COUCH TO THE TOILET
role: Media cartographer; Media War & Peace; co-host The Media Odyssey; former network executive
summary: In a Miami keynote, Shapiro presents cross-screen attention data from 23 regions. Phones beat TV sets for video time by more than two to one in the US, the bedroom is the top place to watch, and 75% of the IPL final was watched on phones. His de-duplicated attention index ranks YouTube first in the US as the only platform strong on both TVs and phones; TikTok wins total attention among under-25s. Subscription streaming added 175 million subscribers last year but lost 156 million, and PwC data shows advertising passing subscriptions in global revenue.
why: A data-heavy case for following the audience across screens, including for sports rights holders.
key_points: Cannibalisation is a myth: CazéTV hit 24 million concurrent YouTube streams for the World Cup final while 70 million watched on broadcast.
Indie creators showed three to five times better engagement quality than mega creators.
Heinz mocking FIFA's stadium branding rules drove about $45 million in earned media and a 12% sales lift.
World of Wonder's fandom-built WOW Presents reports 96% retention.

title: Athletes own the mic now
role: Founder, Notice
summary: Guest writer Tim Ashworth, founder of sport PR agency Loyal, argues athletes now reach fans before any club, broadcaster or agency, so sport PR has to move upstream. His example is Nathan Cleary turning online abuse of an opponent into a sportsmanship story with one post from hospital. Sport is Australia's third-biggest podcast genre (about 3.3 million monthly listeners), and a USC Annenberg study found a third of Gen Z Americans follow individual athletes over teams. The new job is helping talent know its voice, build its own channels (from the 167 Podcast to New Heights' reported US$100 million-plus deal) and pick its moments.
why: Changes how clubs and agencies should staff communications: less writing releases, more preparing athletes who are already their own media channel.

title: Why KevOnStage Makes More Money Performing in Churches
role: Founder, Trapital
summary: Runcie's takeaways from his Trapital Summit conversation with comedian KevOnStage. Touring is still his biggest and best-margin revenue stream, and he can sometimes earn more from 300 tickets at a church than about 1,000 at a big-city venue once venue fees, required staffing, production, ticketing charges and merch cuts are taken out. He runs a deliberately lean tour (himself, a tour manager and a photographer). He treats free social, podcast and Tubi content the way musicians treat streaming: a way to build enough affinity that buying a ticket feels natural. His Tubi deal combines funding with creative control, ownership and backend.
why: A creator-led view of live economics: venue size is not the same as profit, and consistent free content is what fills the room.

title: 185 - How I'd Spend $1,000 on Meta Ads to Generate Group Sales Leads
role: Host, Sports Marketing Machine podcast; 21+ years in sports marketing
summary: Jeremy Neisser lays out how he would spend a $1,000 Meta budget on group sales leads instead of boosting a 'book your group outing' post. The plan: pick one buyer type (for example company outings), mine 15 to 20 real inquiries for their reasons, build three ads around three motivations, and run one lead-generation campaign to a broad local audience. He splits the budget at about $35 a day over four weeks ($800 prospecting, $200 retargeting), uses a Meta instant form, follows up the same day, and judges it on booked outings, revenue and cost per booked group.
why: A ready-to-run, measurable test for one of the most under-marketed ticket revenue lines at clubs and venues.
key_points: You are looking for one organiser for 50 people, not 50 single-ticket buyers, so the targeting and copy differ from individual ticket ads.
Test different reasons to book, not different photos of the same message.
Interest or job-title targeting can miss the HR director who books the outing; she may not be a baseball fan.
His worked example: $1,000 producing 5 booked groups and $3,750 in tickets, which he stresses is not profit.

title: The Atlanta Dream’s WNBA Finals venue snafu goes deeper than a Sombr concert
role: Editor, The Boston Globe; author, The Fixture
summary: The Atlanta Dream nearly played WNBA Finals home games at their 3,500-seat Gateway Center because State Farm Arena had a concert and the Hawks' home opener booked; games were moved only after intense lobbying. McInerney uses it to argue that venue control is the biggest issue facing women's sports. CPKC Stadium in Kansas City is the only purpose-built stadium for a professional women's team, and has sold out every game. A Populous and Project Level report estimates purpose-built venues could unlock $1 billion for a women's team over decades through tickets, suites, sponsorship, parking and fan data, while tenants get second-choice dates that hurt media deals.
why: Frames ownership of the venue, not attendance records, as what turns women's teams into durable businesses.

byline: Dave Siroty (guest post on Joe Favorito's blog)
title: Guest Post: College Athletics Doesn’t Have an Awareness Problem. It Has an Engagement Opportunity
role: Sports marketing and communications strategist; Columbia University lecturer
summary: Watching empty seats at Army football's biggest game of the year, Siroty, a former college sports and Coldwell Banker communications lead, argues college athletics has the brand awareness insurers spend billions to buy but fails to convert it. His rough maths for Army: 4,500 students, 7,000 faculty and staff, 80,000 alumni and 3 million people in the Hudson Valley, against 30,000 at a football game, or about 1% of the potential audience. He calls for marketing teams to move each of five groups (recruits, current fans, new ticket buyers, donors, corporate partners) from awareness to engagement to action, with 'surround sound' marketing across all channels.
why: A simple audience-sizing exercise any club or venue can run to show how much reach it is not converting.

title: Teaching Athletes to Ask: Funding Australia's Olympians - Natalie Cook, Aussie Athlete Fund
role: Founder, Sports Geek
summary: Five-time Olympian Natalie Cook, founder of the Aussie Athlete Fund, argues that athlete funding needs a livable wage, not one-off medal payments. The episode cites 46% of athletes living below the poverty line, and Cook says she retired $300,000 in debt. The fund matches athletes with businesses one-to-many (pitching to 100 businesses at once rather than one sponsorship coffee at a time), runs a $1 million challenge, and routes support through the Australian Sports Foundation so it is tax deductible.
why: A corporate-backed funding model for Olympic athletes ahead of Brisbane 2032, with clear hooks for sponsors.
key_points: Supporters can get regular athlete appearances (morning teas, trivia, annual functions) in return.
She does not see funding as purely government's job: if 1,000 Australian businesses each funded one full-time role, the problem would largely be solved.
IOC Rule 40 limits on athlete sponsorship are loosening, which opens longer-term brand partnerships.
'Asking is free': she argues asking for support is a skill athletes can be taught.

title: The Nashville Symphony: Deficit-Crisis-Miracle
role: Writes Talking Tickets!, a newsletter for people who sell tickets to live events: sports, concerts, opera and entertainment
summary: Part 3 of Wakeman's series on the Nashville Symphony. Oracle's $10M gift saved the 2026 season, but he argues it is the third rescue in thirteen years: the building was in foreclosure in 2013 until Martha Ingram stepped in, and COVID relief of more than $16M covered 2020. Expenses exceeded revenues by $39M from 2009 to 2012 (an $11.7M loss in 2012 alone) and again from 2014 to 2019, with deficits returning once relief ended. He compares the pattern to WeWork's repeated restarts and ends with a five-question sustainability audit.
why: A clear warning for any venue or event organisation that a donor or bail-out has quietly become its operating model.

title: Who Prints Media Guides and Notes In A Growing Digital World? No One Seemed To Know, So We Asked…
role: Sports marketing and communications strategist; Columbia University lecturer
summary: Noticing bare press-box shelves at the World Cup, Favorito's team surveyed the 122 clubs in the four major US leagues about printed media guides, game notes and rosters, a question the leagues said nobody had asked. Fewer than half still print media guides: most MLB clubs do, over two thirds of NFL clubs print limited runs, the NBA is about evenly split, and only six NHL respondents printed guides this year. Drivers include budgets, fewer accredited media, video-first creators, remote broadcasts fed digitally, and California rules limiting printing. Yet printed rosters and small programs for fans appear to have risen.
why: Original data on how team communications operations are going digital, and where print still earns its cost.

title: The NBA Is Putting Microchips Inside Basketballs
role: Founder, Huddle Up newsletter; sports business writer and investor
summary: Adam Silver says NBA basketballs will carry Bluetooth tracking chips from as soon as 2027, following the NFL, where chips in balls and shoulder pads plus Hawk-Eye cameras feed Next Gen Stats for teams, broadcasters and fans. The players' union has kept body-worn trackers optional, and teams can be fined up to $250,000 for using such data in contract talks. Pompliano's point is that those rules cover players, not the ball, which the league has been developing with Wilson for years.
why: Shows how a league can build a data product for broadcast and fan engagement while working around union limits on player-worn tracking.

title: Team Vitality Is Betting on Its Own Brand in China as Part of Its Asian Expansion
role: Esports and gaming marketing agency founder; lecturer; 20+ years in esports
summary: Team Vitality is building its own brand in China instead of the usual Western route of partnering with a local organisation (PSG.LGD, G2.iG, Wolves Weibo eSports). It launched on RedNote in September (6,000+ followers and 1.6 million exposures in a month), ran a 'Vitality Eastbound' meet-and-greet with partner Evnia that sold out in hours, and has grown Weibo, Douyin and Bilibili channels to over 600,000 followers since the 2024 Shanghai Major. In Southeast Asia, by contrast, it bought Bigetron and kept its local identity.
why: Two different market-entry models from the same team: acquire and keep the local brand, or build your own through local platforms, merchandise and fan events.

title: What will happen with the WTA, and lessons from the ATP
role: Sportfolio; teaches private equity investing at Oxford; former Wall Street bank investor; PE co-founder
summary: Former banker and PE executive Vuković compares the two tennis tours' finances. The ATP took a Saudi PIF partnership, centralised media and data rights under ATP Media through its OneVision reforms, and offered players 50/50 profit sharing on audited Masters 1000 results. That has paid out $49 million since 2022 and taken revenue from $144 million (2018) to $294 million (2024), with $52 million net income. The WTA sold 20% of its commercial arm to CVC for $150 million over five years, but recorded a $5 million loss in 2024, and the Telegraph projects a $23 million loss and $15 million in cash for 2026 after the Riyadh Finals ended. Vuković argues the real failure is not the roughly $30 million a year spent topping up prize money but that revenue barely grew, from $103 million to a projected $112 million.
why: A clear case study of governance reform, transparency and topline growth deciding who wins between two rights holders with similar products.

title: UP575 Chat_UP: 'That's So AI', Rogue Agents and Superintelligence
role: Owner and editor, Unofficial Partner
summary: Gillis and Andy Shora of TFG Labs ask what Gen Z's insult 'that's so AI' means for a sports industry selling AI to investors, sponsors and fans at once. Per a PTI Digital benchmark, 81% of UK rights holders use AI but only a third strategically. They discuss who should own AI inside a club, and AI becoming a shirt sponsorship category as gambling leaves Premier League shirts, including what happens to a club's tech stack when an AI shirt deal ends. They also cover why autonomous agents raise the risk from bad copy to switched-off turnstiles.
why: Raises the governance questions clubs should settle before an AI vendor becomes both sponsor and infrastructure.
key_points: Fans discount content that looks machine-made; craft and effort still win attention.
Clubs are now being asked what their AI spend has returned as hyperscaler capex passes $1 trillion.
Relying on a model that a government could switch off is a supply risk for match-day operations.
Open-weight and smaller local models can do some jobs for a fraction of the cost.

title: Inside On’s Go-to-Market Masterclass in Football
role: Founder and writer, Sportsverse; award-winning business journalist
summary: Miller breaks down how On is entering football after signing Kylian Mbappé from Nike, rather than following the usual 'sign in secret, reveal with the product' formula. Its approach has four linked parts: a fly-on-the-wall On Football account (380,000 followers within weeks), coded prototype boots worn in matches that unlock exclusive content online, a clear role for each ambassador (Thierry Henry as statesman, Sydney Schertenleib for a women's boot at the 2027 Women's World Cup), and its LightSpray robotic manufacturing as the visible technology story. The first boot is not due until 2027.
why: A blueprint for turning one big athlete signing into a long-running content and fan-engagement campaign, rather than a single announcement.

title: The ISL is in its clubs’ hands
role: Founder, The State of Play; The Left Field
summary: The Indian Super League has started its first club-run season: the 13 clubs control its commercial business through a jointly owned company, and the AIFF takes 10% of net profits. All 163 matches stream free on YouTube worldwide, with Sony showing 80+ on TV and SonyLIV carrying the full season behind its paywall. Clubs were split, with most backing YouTube's reach and a few wanting TV to protect sponsorship. The opening weekend drew close to 45 million YouTube views, and clubs now get state-by-state viewing data. The issue also covers Everton's owners exploring a sale at about £800 million including £380 million of debt.
why: A live test of whether free, global YouTube distribution and club-owned data can out-earn a conventional paywalled rights deal.

byline: Simon Chadwick (Forbes column, shared on LinkedIn)
limitations: Forbes may meter access; the same essay is free on the GeoSport Substack (19 Oct).
title: F1 Highlights The Realities Of Global Sport's Chokepoint Problems
role: Professor of Sport and Geopolitical Economy, SKEMA Business School
summary: Chadwick argues that narrow sea passages thousands of miles away now shape event hosting, revenues and kit supply. F1's cancelled Bahrain and Saudi races this year cost hosts an estimated $120 million+, and Bahrain paid Malaysia about $68 million in hosting and rights fees to keep its race on the calendar. Qatar and Abu Dhabi are still exposed, as is the 2027 Basketball World Cup in Doha. Beyond Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab, he flags the Strait of Malacca: Vietnam makes up to a billion pairs of sports shoes a year, including about 50% of Nike's footwear and up to 40% of Adidas's, most of it shipped West through that strait.
why: A reminder that event calendars, host deals and merchandise supply all carry geopolitical risk that needs contingency planning.

title: The D2C Delusion: Why Owning an Audience might be Sports Most Expensive Lie
role: Writes The Black Book; former head of Australasia for Bleacher Report/TNT Sports, interim media and communications manager for SANZAAR and CMO of BLK Sport
summary: Mortimer argues the push to 'own the fan' through proprietary apps and gated D2C services has mostly built databases, not communities. He points to WWE closing its standalone network after reaching about 1.5 million subscribers, then licensing to Peacock, Netflix ($5bn over 10 years) and ESPN ($1.6bn); the NFL putting Sunday Ticket on YouTube for about $2bn a year; and UFC's $7.7bn Paramount deal. His case is that open platforms create the social conditions in which fan communities form.
why: A strong challenge to registration counts as a success metric, for anyone planning a club or league digital strategy.

title: How Nike Broke Its Own Business
role: Founder, Huddle Up newsletter; sports business writer and investor
summary: Pompliano argues Nike's slide (shares down about 80% from their pandemic peak, China sales down 30% since 2021) is not about politics or a lack of innovation. The public part covers the first cause: CEO John Donahoe's push to sell direct to customers for margin and data pulled product from long-time retailers, who filled the shelf space with Hoka, Brooks and On. The other causes he names (Jordan Brand, China, heavy discounting) are behind the paywall.
why: A clear warning for any rights holder going direct to fans: intermediaries also create demand, and losing them can cost more than the margin you gain.

title: Does Live Nation Top Boss Michael Rapino Deserve $60 Million A Year + Why Robert Kraft Is Afraid to Treat Zach Bryan Like He Treated Ed Sheeran
role: Senior Director, Live Music and Touring, Billboard; founder Decibel
summary: Brooks and entertainment attorney Michael Seville cover three stories. Robert Kraft removed Macklemore from Ed Sheeran's Gillette Stadium show over a 'Free Palestine' remark but said nothing when record-setting Zach Bryan wore the same message, which they put down to box office. Live Nation has doubled Michael Rapino's target pay to $60 million a year through 2031 (about $320 million over five years with a signing grant), with unusually friendly vesting terms. The US Copyright Office has opened an inquiry into fake streams and AI tracks draining royalty pools.
why: Shows how venue owners' stated principles bend to ticket sales, and what the market leader's board is rewarding during its antitrust remedies fight.
key_points: Rapino's package is about $20 million cash (salary plus a bonus on adjusted operating income) and $40 million in stock tied to top-quartile S&P 500 performance.
The standout terms are time-based vesting, payouts lockable after two years, vesting at target if he is pushed out, and Live Nation paying his own lawyers.
Deezer reports up to 85% of streams on AI-generated music were fraudulent; the hosts suggest streaming services may not welcome scrutiny of inflated engagement.

title: Aron McGuire on Building Commercial Resilience in Olympic Sport
role: Founder, Berkida Ventures; The Berkida Brief
summary: USA Bobsled & Skeleton CEO Aron McGuire explains how a governing body with no government funding runs on grants, sponsors and donors. Its strategic plan, built with athletes, coaches, board and partners, acts as the filter for every budget call. Instead of fixed sponsorship packages, it starts from each partner's business and gives partners a role in performance: Under Armour on apparel, Honda on aerodynamics, Snowflake on data analytics, Raising Cane's on promotion and athlete recruitment. The commercial job is turning the Olympic-year spike in attention into multi-year engagement.
why: A small rights holder's playbook for sponsorship as a value exchange: partners who contribute capability are stickier than logo buyers.

title: 184 - How to Improve Group Sales Marketing & Meta Ads
role: Host, Sports Marketing Machine podcast; 21+ years in sports marketing
summary: Part one of Neisser's group sales series applies Eugene Schwartz's five stages of awareness (from Breakthrough Advertising) to selling group outings. He argues a 'book your group outing' post only reaches people who have already decided. Teams should instead write for each stage and buyer: an HR director planning staff appreciation, a church administrator, a team mum or a business owner entertaining clients. That runs from 'Your employees deserve more than another pizza party' to 'Request available dates'.
why: A simple copy framework for group and hospitality sales that most teams skip.
key_points: Many people in a market know the team but not that it offers group outings, so early-stage copy has to plant the idea.
Meta cannot target by awareness stage; use the stages as a messaging framework instead.
Five graphics with the same message are still one message.
Group sales calls, emails and form submissions are the best source of ad copy, and AI tools can help turn them into drafts.

title: College Sports Has Been A Business Violating the Laws of Congress for More than a Century
role: Sports economist; author of The Wages of Wins, Stumbling on Wins and Sports Economics, and more than 90 academic articles
summary: Berri argues the NCAA has run a buyers' cartel (a monopsony) over athlete labour for more than a century while lobbying Congress for antitrust immunity. He notes the NCAA's own figure that 98% of 550,000 athletes never turn professional, so it is the only sports employer most will have. He rebuts the main defences: profits are meaningless for non-profits, the money has gone to coaches and facilities ($185M paid to fired coaches by week ten of 2025), pay limits have not produced balance (73% of Division I basketball schools have never reached a Final Four), and college sport is small within universities (Ohio State: $336M of $8.5bn).
why: Clear economic arguments on athlete pay rules, relevant wherever leagues use caps or eligibility rules to hold down labour costs.

limitations: The lawsuit details and catalogue estimates are Gouveia's figures; not independently checked.
title: The AI Purge Has Begun
role: Toronto-based artist manager and sync rep; co-founder of Sincerely Management, Fivepin Music and Sellout.fm; writes The Artist Economy
summary: Gouveia explains why DistroKid began mass-removing tracks flagged as AI, using the case of independent artist Josh Sahunta, whose 2023 album was taken down with no appeal route. As he reports it, Universal Music Group sued DistroKid on 15 September 2026 seeking $150,000 per infringing song, while a human artist pays DistroKid about $25 a year. That asymmetry, roughly 6,000 to 1, pushes the distributor to delete first. He adds that even a detector at Deezer's claimed 99.8% accuracy would wrongly flag about 120,000 of the roughly 60 million songs DistroKid has delivered.
why: Shows how liability, not accuracy, sets platform policy, and how independent creators carry the cost when rights holders sue the pipes.

title: NBA Faces Uphill Battle In Fight For Future Of European Basketball
role: Sports and business journalist, Sprungstack; formerly Boardroom, Forbes, Awful Announcing
summary: After meeting at Lake Como, the EuroLeague rejected the NBA's takeover proposal and gave its 13 licensed clubs permanent status instead of 10-year contracts, tabling expansion to as many as 21 clubs. The NBA's offer was reportedly well below the $3 billion EuroLeague values itself at, and some stakeholders called it 'colonialist'. NBA Europe's launch could slip from 2027 to 2028, and at least six EuroLeague clubs, including Real Madrid and Bayern Munich, are reportedly considering defecting. Sprung concludes there is almost certainly not room for two premier leagues in the same cities, so the NBA may need to raise its offer or face a long war.
why: Explains the stand-off between an incumbent league and a cash-rich entrant, useful for anyone weighing a breakaway or a merger.

byline: Evan Shapiro and Marion Ranchet (The Media Odyssey)
title: HOW TO FIX KIDS CONTENT
role: Media cartographer; Media War & Peace; co-host The Media Odyssey; former network executive
summary: Kids media analyst Emily Horgan, discussing her Netflix kids content report, argues Netflix is 'the stage, not the lab'. Its kids hits mostly started five or more years ago or were built on YouTube (Ms. Rachel, digital-first animation), and it licenses proven IP rather than creating characters. YouTube's kids ad revenue has collapsed in five years after COPPA enforcement and advertiser caution, even though kids content is about 15% of platform usage, throttling the pipeline that produced Cocomelon. Durable franchises 20+ years old dominate, and new shows can take 28 months or more to find an audience.
why: The audience-first playbook for IP applies to any entertainment brand trying to build a franchise.
key_points: AI-assisted studios like Toonstar cut animation costs to about 5% of traditional levels, but 'AI slop' erodes parents' trust.
The winning model is audience first: build direct fan relationships through YouTube, live events and merch before seeking distribution.
Steven and Parker reach 30 million weekly viewers across six languages; Sesame Street windows between Netflix and YouTube.

byline: Jack Cheal and Harry Greenwood (guest writers)
title: How to unlock the value of your fan base
role: Founder, Notice
summary: Guest writers Jack Cheal of Sports Cloud Australia (the NRL's data partner) and Harry Greenwood of the NRL describe joining up more than six million first-party fan records across ticketing, membership, merchandise, apps and digital. The aim was an individual-level view of each fan: how often they engage, which touchpoints matter, and what they spend over time. That let the NRL segment fans by engagement level and value, and open partner conversations with the slice of the audience a brand actually wants, rather than total audience size.
why: A worked example of turning a large fan database into a commercial asset for partnership sales. Written by the vendor and its client, so treat it as a case study rather than an independent review.

title: Rugby League Is About to Find Out If the World Gives a Damn
role: Writes The Black Book; former head of Australasia for Bleacher Report/TNT Sports, interim media and communications manager for SANZAAR and CMO of BLK Sport
summary: Ahead of the 2026 Rugby League World Cup in Australia and Papua New Guinea, Mortimer weighs the decision to cut the field from 16 nations to 10. He sets out the gap between the NRL, with a seven-year $5.3bn rights deal, an $11.95M top-30 salary cap and about $18M in annual grants per club, and England's Super League, with a £2.1M cap. The 2021 tournament barely cleared £20M, and he asks whether the sport's passion, especially in PNG, can be turned into an international product.
why: A clear case study of event format, scarcity and money as levers for growing an international competition.

title: Padel and pickleball: what makes a fast-growing sport last?
role: Partner, CAA Portas (Dubai)
summary: From a SPORTBIZ Europe panel, Drentje tests racket-sport hype against CAA Portas data. Padel has 35 million players (up 133% since 2020) and pickleball 24 million (up 500%), both about 40% women. But two in three US pickleball players played fewer than eight times last year, while 92% of people who try padel come back. Profitability drives supply: one tennis court becomes three padel or four pickleball courts, and padel lifts daily revenue 5 to 7 times. About half of market value sits in clubs and courts, needing US$17 to 20 billion by 2035.
why: Useful for venue operators and investors weighing court conversions or new participation sports.
key_points: Building without demand leads to closures, as in Sweden and Chile: 'growth is global; value is local'.
Padel has one world federation and an Olympic path; pickleball still has rival world bodies and calendars.
His own answer: governance first, because courts can be built anywhere and data can be bought.

title: Why Formula 1 Makes So Much Sense for Revolut
role: Founder and publisher, Faze 3 Sport; Culture of Sport and Original Football
summary: Skilling argues Revolut's title partnership with the Audi F1 team goes deeper than exposure. Revolut Business runs the team's finances, Revolut Pay powers its merchandise sales, and a new team-branded payment card puts the partnership in fans' wallets. The fit, he says, is that F1 tours many of the markets where Revolut is building one global financial brand (80 million customers, targeting 100 million by mid-2027), including the US, where it has conditional approval for a national bank planned for 2027.
why: A model for a sponsor that embeds in a team's operations and products, so the partnership builds market entry rather than just awareness.

title: Building Technology That Works Like a Light Switch - Ronnie Bryant, Charlotte Hornets
role: Founder, Sports Geek
summary: Charlotte Hornets CIO Ronnie Bryant, 22 years with the franchise from its expansion era, shares lessons from running technology at Spectrum Center. The arena had stadium-wide Wi-Fi when it opened in 2005, but its 80 access points could not cope once the iPhone arrived in 2007. His biggest lesson is to invest while the walls are still open, because retrofitting can cost twice as much. The Hornets have now finished a Wi-Fi 7 rollout with naming-rights partner Spectrum Enterprise, which Bryant says is its first deployment in the country.
why: Practical capital-planning advice for any venue weighing technology spend during a build or renovation.
key_points: Good venue technology should work like a light switch: redundancy and reliability are what build trust.
The business intelligence team has doubled as the arena hosts far more concerts, family shows and conventions, not just basketball.
Coaching and high-performance staff are a different kind of client from fans.
NBA team technology leaders work together like a shared R&D group.

limitations: The full essay requires a free sign-up; this summary is based on the publicly readable opening and the author's own summary.
title: Creating Pull
role: The Mediator; former EVP and Chief Strategy Officer, Turner, 2015 to 2018 (verified)
summary: Doug Shapiro argues that consumers will increasingly hand AI agents and chatbots the work of choosing what to watch, read, listen to and play, continuing a decades-long decline in distributors' control. Unlike distributors, agents have no stake in promoting any particular content. He cites Bain (16% of consumers, 25% of Gen Z, have fully replaced search with chatbots), Pew (1% click-through when an AI Overview appears) and Meta Muse's 2.8 million downloads in 12 days. His answer is demand pull: brands, IP, talent and above all communities, which generate the signals AI uses and make fans seek content out directly. Creators are built around communities; traditional media is built around campaigns.
why: Rights holders and entertainment brands face the same shift: if agents choose, community is the moat.

title: The Yankees Have A “Sequel” That’s A Marketing First…
role: Sports marketing and communications strategist; Columbia University lecturer
summary: The New York Yankees' deal with Sequel, the first tampon brand to partner with an MLB team, is put in historical context. In 1995 the WTA Tour turned down a three-year, $10 million title sponsorship from Tampax maker Tambrands for fear of ridicule and sponsor backlash, then signed Corel for less a year later. Favorito says the deal reflects teams treating women as a significant audience for men's sport. Sequel, founded by two former athletes and backed by more than $8 million in funding, built credibility through D.C. United, the Indiana Fever and Athletes Unlimited venues before stepping up to the Yankees.
why: A neat example of a sponsor category once seen as too risky becoming mainstream, and of a challenger brand climbing the ladder of rights holders.

title: 5 takeaways from Converge summit
role: Founder and editor, Stadium Tech Report
summary: Kerravala's five takeaways from Stadium Tech Report's Converge summit are mostly about money. Technology has grown to about 20% of a new stadium's build cost while venue revenue grows about 5% a year, and refreshing systems across about 144 major North American venues implies about $10 billion of replacement spend over the next decade. AmpThink's Bill Anderson calls the Wi-Fi vs DAS debate a vendor's question; the owner's question is total connectivity cost and what it returns. Converged networks are proven, and one venue cut its switches from more than 500 to about 300 and saved $2.4 million in hardware. The blocker is procurement: stadium specs are split across 47 divisions, each owned by a party protecting its own scope.
why: The clearest recent case that venue technology ROI should be argued on operating profit and event utilisation, not 'fan experience'.
key_points: A Midwest build used integrated delivery to cut about 4% of construction cost and replaced a $1.5M control room with a hired truck at about $20,000 per event.
Cheaper activation lets venues run more small events: in the example, contribution per event dollar rises from about 20 to 45 cents.
One attendee is adding a 10% AI cost-inflation contingency on top of normal escalation, citing GPU and storage prices and generator lead times.
Advice: own your entry points and fiber, fund adoption as a marketing line, and contribute to shared benchmarks.

title: A new generation of stadium builders
role: Founder and editor, Stadium Tech Report
summary: Stadium Tech Report modelled how often sports executives actually build a stadium. At about four new major-league venues a year (95 since 1999), an executive with a 25-year career has about a 46% chance of being at a club during a new build. With 20 to 27 North American stadiums of 10,000+ seats potentially opening from 2027 to 2030, a pace of six a year would lift that to about 63%. Of 50 owner-side executives on current projects whose records could be classified, 25 had no comparable project on record. Finance showed the biggest gap: eight of nine finance leaders had none.
why: Shows that most stadium builds are run by first-timers and where the experience gaps are, which matters to anyone selling into or running a new venue.
key_points: About 42% of team presidents in the big five US leagues have spent their whole sports career at one organisation.
An estimated 140 to 180 owner-side people steer the 15 to 20 active stadium programs in a typical year.
Design choices made to save capital can raise operating costs for decades, and in-building systems turn over several times in a stadium's life.
Clubs like the Titans deliberately hire repeat builders; Buffalo used fan feedback on the old stadium to set technology priorities.

title: How Undead Labs saved itself and State of Decay from oblivion
role: Leads The Game Business; previously nine years at MCV and over eight years as head of GamesIndustry.biz
summary: Undead Labs head Philip Holt explains how the State of Decay studio bought itself out of Xbox after a planned sale fell through, then laid off a significant number of staff. He describes nervous capital waiting for obvious hits, investor scrutiny of Seattle labour costs against cheaper regions, and the shift from a first-party tentpole thesis to an independent company that must survive on its own revenue.
why: A practical look at financing and cost structure when a creative business leaves a corporate parent.
key_points: A management buyout replaced the expected buyer; State of Decay 3 now has a new, unnamed publisher.
Investors weighed team cost and decision speed; challenges made it easy to say no.
Holt declined to give layoff numbers but says the game, in alpha, did not need a radical rescope.

title: Does The WNBA Need Caitlin Clark In The Finals To Reach Its Full Potential?
role: Sports and business journalist, Sprungstack; formerly Boardroom, Forbes, Awful Announcing
summary: Caitlin Clark's Indiana Fever went out in the first round even though the deciding game averaged 2.25 million viewers on USA Network, so Sprung asks how much the WNBA's TV growth depends on one player. The regular season averaged 771,000 viewers (up 17%, the best since 2000), with 51 games topping a million. Every ESPN/ABC game above 2 million featured the Fever, though Disney's non-Fever games were still up 24%. His verdict: the league grows without Clark, but much more slowly, and splitting the Finals so the less-watched USA Network carries five of the seven games adds risk.
why: Hard numbers on star dependence and what it means for a women's league's media value.

title: The Most Important Media CEO Resume Doesn’t Look Like a Media CEO Resume
role: Disruptive Play; co-founder Creator Sports Network
summary: Cohen reads Ynon Kreiz's appointment as co-CEO of the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery (running operations and integration under David Ellison) as a signal of what a modern media leader needs. Each step of his career maps to a force reshaping the business: Fox Kids Europe (distribution across markets), Balderton (technology), Endemol (formats that repeat across countries), Maker Studios (creators who own the audience relationship) and Mattel (franchises such as Barbie spanning film, games and experiences). He draws the sports parallels: leagues are repeatable formats, and creators should be part of distribution strategy, not just marketing.
why: A useful lens for sports executives: the skills to lead now are distribution, creators and franchise-building, not just rights deals.

title: #14: Ronaldo, creators and a RSL scorecard: what's next for Saudi football?
role: Riyadh-based commercial, digital and data lead (Expo 2030 Riyadh); Sports Signal
summary: Istvanova covers three Saudi football stories. A RedBird-led US-Saudi consortium, reportedly including Ronaldo as an investor, is negotiating with PIF for a stake in Al Nassr; with Al Kholood, Al Hilal and others, privatisation is following several models. A Bain and Twenty First Group outside-in scorecard shows follower growth slowing to 3%, attendance down 7% to about 7,800 (mostly from one club, Al Ittihad), and a 111% premium on domestic transfers. And the Saudi Pro League now lets any approved creator, player or club sell live matches on a revenue-share basis in 16 markets via Recast, going direct where broadcast deals were built for exposure rather than money (DAZN's UK deal was reportedly about $500k).
why: The creator pay-per-view model is a new distribution play any league with low-value overseas rights could test.

title: Why now may be the best time for Portugal to move beyond Cristiano Ronaldo
role: Founder, Sport by Fort; former VP Global Sports and Entertainment Partnerships (head of global sponsorships), Coca-Cola, 2016 to 2021 (verified)
summary: Former Coca-Cola and Visa global sponsorship chief Ricardo Fort argues that, if Portugal can do without Cristiano Ronaldo on the pitch, now is the commercially right time to move on. For years Ronaldo gave brands a reason to sponsor Portugal that few national teams could match, but co-hosting the 2030 World Cup gives the federation a new story to sell: participating in a defining national moment. Not every sponsor will stay, and hosting does not replace his global reach, but it lets the FPF build its next commercial chapter from a position of strength while demand has another reason to grow.
why: A practical frame for any rights holder whose commercial programme leans on one star: time the transition to a new demand driver.

title: How Fulham FC is Differentiating from their Piers... 🚣
role: Managing Director, TPF Labs, The Players Fund; Sports Pundit
summary: Fulham Pier has opened Sael, a four-floor luxury spa inside Fulham's new Riverside Stand, alongside a hotel, restaurants, a food market and a members' club. Per Fulham Pier director Glen Sutton, the development was planned around the roughly 340 days a year without a home match, and he expects 50 to 60% of its revenue to come from non-matchdays. The stand lifts Craven Cottage to about 28,800 seats and premium seating from about 1.5% to 10% of capacity.
why: A mid-table club that cannot match the giants on broadcast or tickets is building revenue with no link to either, using the stadium as one part of a year-round destination.

title: Did Anthropic Use Torrents and Illegal Downloading To Steal Song Lyrics + Deep Dive on Ari Emanuel's New Book Roll The Calls
role: Senior Director, Live Music and Touring, Billboard; founder Decibel
summary: Brooks and attorney Michael Seville examine Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell's lawsuit against Anthropic, which alleges more than 20,000 songs' lyrics and sheet music were used to train its models, sourced partly via torrenting from pirate libraries, and which names its CEO and co-founder personally. They explain why acquisition, not training, is the weak point, citing the Bartz authors' case that ended in a $1.5 billion settlement. They also cover 20 states plus DC seeking records of Live Nation's DOJ settlement negotiations, and a light segment on Ari Emanuel's memoir.
why: Where the money in music rights and AI is likely to be decided: in how training data was obtained.
key_points: The publishers seek up to $150,000 per work in statutory damages; Anthropic says training is transformative fair use.
In Bartz, Judge Alsup found training could be fair use but acquiring works through piracy was not.
Under the Tunney Act the judge could treat the DOJ settlement as a floor and add remedies; Seville now thinks a Ticketmaster divestiture is more likely.

title: Manchester City and Football’s Financial Rules
role: Founder, Berkida Ventures; The Berkida Brief
summary: Marinelli explains what the Premier League commission found against Manchester City for 2009/10 to 2017/18: certain sponsorship receipts were really owner funding that should have been recorded as equity, alongside other revenue and cost misstatements, together inflating revenue and cutting costs by more than £900m (a combined figure, not a fine). City rejects the findings and will appeal. He draws three lessons: fair market value for related-party deals needs judgement, sporting justice has to be faster, and accounting-based rules can distort incentives, which squad-cost ratios may not fully fix.
why: The case turns on how sponsorship from owner-linked companies is valued, which every club with related-party deals now needs to get right.

title: How Sports Teams Price and Sell Digital Sponsorship Inventory
role: Writes The Commercial Table, interviews and breakdowns for commercial and marketing teams at rights holders, brands and suppliers in sport
summary: Singh interviews Alex Kopilow, who grew the Chicago White Sox's digital revenue by 62% in a year and later closed the largest digital deal in New York Mets history. Kopilow argues most teams have 20 to 40 sellable digital ideas when they should have about 200, and that digital has been treated as a throw-in after signage, hospitality and naming rights. He explains how he helped Dagenham & Redbridge build 149 ideas valued at £3M, the inputs he uses to price a content series, and why sponsored content fails when it is not what fans expected.
why: A practical method for turning a club's existing content into priced sponsorship inventory.

title: Star power matters
role: Founder, Notice
summary: Notice contrasts the AFL's Kylie Minogue Grand Final partnership with the NRL's decision to skip a headline act, after Peter V'landys questioned paying '$100,000 a minute'. Announced six months out, Kylie became a campaign: a merchandise range, a Footy Fest store, a 13-storey mural, coverage in Vogue and Rolling Stone, and brand tie-ins from Telstra, Sherrin (a sold-out Kylie football), Specsavers and Tiffany. The Grand Final averaged 4.52 million viewers, the most-watched on record, 98,000 fans were inside the MCG an hour early to see her, and her posts out-engaged match posts on the day (279,000 vs 248,000).
why: Judging a headline act on cost per minute misses most of its value: the months-long platform it gives the event, partners and new audiences.

title: Talking to NBC News about Major League Baseball and How the Owners are Wrong about a Salary Cap (again!)
role: Sports economist; author of The Wages of Wins, Stumbling on Wins and Sports Economics, and more than 90 academic articles
summary: Berri shares his full answers to NBC News on whether MLB teams can buy titles. From 2011 to 2025, payroll relative to the league average explained only 14% of the variation in winning percentage (12% in 2026 to 22 September), and 15-year cumulative spending explained 30% of cumulative wins. In 2025 the Dodgers spent $411M against a $178M average and won 93 games, while the Brewers spent about $123M and won 97. He attributes this to randomness, smaller talent gaps from global scouting, and six years of team control over young players.
why: Evidence for the salary-cap debate: in baseball, spending buys far less success than owners claim.

title: Oligopoly Go!
role: Co-founder of SuperData Research (acquired by Nielsen); teaches the Business of Video Games at NYU Stern; author of One Up
summary: Using his dataset of 153 game companies (109 listed, 44 private), van Dreunen measures how concentrated games publishing has become over 15 years. The ten largest publishers now take 56% of publishing revenue, up from a low of 45% in 2020 but below 65% in 2010, and the four largest hold 39%. Console concentration reached 1,400 on his concentration index in the year the Activision Blizzard deal closed and sits at 1,304; five firms take 74% of console revenue. He predicts the top ten will control two-thirds of revenue by 2030, arguing AI may widen who makes games but not who makes money from them.
why: Original data on market power in games, useful context for anyone negotiating with publishers, platforms or rights owners in gaming.

title: Bundle economics came for RSNs first; national rights rely on the same dollars
role: Sports media consultant; former SVP Programming, Research and Content Strategy, FOX Sports, 2010 to 2016 (verified)
summary: Former Fox Sports strategy executive Patrick Crakes warns that the shrinking pay-TV bundle money that hollowed out regional sports networks also funds national rights, so adding up every property's hopes of doubling their deals is not a sensible base case. Higher fees may need more partners, platforms, windows and inventory, and digital buyers are now capital-heavy and indebted while media consolidation cuts margins. His opportunity: game-related content works with social and navigation discovery platforms to reach the general market again, and those platforms can answer 'where do I watch?' and route fans to games.
why: A sober counterweight to rights-fee optimism, with a concrete alternative: treat discovery as both reach and distribution.

limitations: Relies on reported internal projections; figures are as Mortimer cites them.
title: Love-Deuce-Bankrupt: A field guide to what happens when sport spends venture money like revenue
role: Writes The Black Book; former head of Australasia for Bleacher Report/TNT Sports, interim media and communications manager for SANZAAR and CMO of BLK Sport
summary: Mortimer examines how the WTA reached a projected financial cliff in 2027 despite record audiences (1.1 billion cumulative viewers, up 10%). He cites operating losses heading towards $23M, cash reserves near $15M by year end, and dependence on CVC's $150M for a 20% stake in WTA Ventures, signed in 2023 and paid in instalments. He argues the money largely funded operations and a fast move to equal prize money without matching commercial growth, compounded by moving the WTA Finals from Saudi Arabia to Indian Wells at the tour's own cost.
why: Shows the risk of using private equity money to fund operating costs, a live question for many rights holders.

title: Building a Team-Based Surfing League - Chris Mater, Surfing Super League
role: Founder, Sports Geek
summary: Surfing Super League CEO Chris Mater, formerly at Red Bull for nearly two decades, explains how he is building a team-based surf league from scratch. Instead of multi-day contests that run seven to nine hours a day, it has eight teams across eight beaches and a 90-minute, made-for-TV format modelled on the length and rhythm of an NRL game. The whole competition was designed backwards from a broadcast window, locked 4pm weekend slots on Fox Sports and Kayo, and borrows the Magic Round and Gather Round idea of a whole-season event.
why: A clean example of designing a new competition around broadcast and commercial needs first.
key_points: Designing from the broadcast window solves surfing's 'holding period' problem, where live TV cannot plan around waiting for waves.
Four commercial pillars: league partners, team partners, host cities, and a minority investor in the league.
The league owns all the franchises, which Mater calls 'a franchise factory', and is watching the Big Bash privatisation as a valuation signal.
He argues a domestic league, not the world tour, will become the most important thing in Australian surfing.

title: Tencent’s bid to create the next FromSoftware and Larian
role: Leads The Game Business; previously nine years at MCV and over eight years as head of GamesIndustry.biz
summary: Tencent Games VP Yong-yi Zhu, who oversees about 20 international studios, explains how Tencent takes Chinese games abroad and backs studios for the long term. Chinese developers have shifted from mobile to console and PC since Black Myth: Wukong, and Tencent publishes regionally, finding pockets where a game resonates rather than adapting everything.
why: An investor's view of patient capital and regional publishing, relevant to anyone building or funding entertainment IP.
key_points: Tencent backs studios that can become category leaders over several games, citing the paths to Baldur's Gate 3 and Elden Ring.
Its studio heads were more open to AI tools than Zhu expected, mostly for concept art, rigging, mocap and code review.
Teams in risky early phases are advised to stay small for longer.

title: What G2 Esports Gets Right About Modern Esports Sponsorships
role: Esports and gaming marketing agency founder; lecturer; 20+ years in esports
summary: Top esports main partnerships now run well beyond $1 million a year, so teams have built marketing departments and even in-house agencies to service them, and want deals lasting years (Team Liquid and Alienware are close to 20). Decker highlights G2 Esports' annual Partners Summit at the LEC finals in Nice, where sponsors including Red Bull, Logitech G, Winamax, Jägermeister and AOC discussed G2's plans and their own goals. CEO Alban Dechelotte says the aim is a partner strategy kept as independent as possible from results on the field.
why: A simple retention tactic any rights holder can copy: bring key sponsors together to align goals, separate from the sporting result.

title: What kind of capital does European football really want?
role: Football commercial adviser; CEO and managing director, AC Milan, Apr 2017 to Aug 2018 (verified)
summary: Former AC Milan and Inter executive Marco Fassone uses the Manchester City verdict to argue that European football's financial rules should separate capital that puts the club at risk from capital that puts the investor at risk. Debt, liquidity, solvency and related-party deals must stay tightly controlled and false reporting severely punished. But an owner who covers sustained losses with genuine new equity, at his own risk, should be allowed to invest. Punish past misconduct, he says, but redesign future rules so they protect sustainability and fair competition, not the existing hierarchy from new challengers.
why: A clear framing for the investor-versus-club risk debate as English and European regulators rewrite their rules.

title: The Cheapest Guest
role: Writes Per Cap on the economics of themed entertainment; 12+ years in investment banking, private credit and corporate development
summary: Vo compares two second-gate theme parks that opened in 2001. On a comparable park-and-hotel basis, Disney's California Adventure needed about $225 of inflation-adjusted opening capital per stabilised annual visitor, while Tokyo DisneySea, a ¥335 billion project, needed about $413. California Adventure drew about 5.6 million visits a year, below expectations, because it asked Disneyland guests to accept a thinner product next door to the original; DisneySea spent to feel distinct enough to justify another ticket. He traces how Disney later had to reinvest to fix the gap.
why: A sharp lesson for any second venue, event or product launched next to a proven one: the cheaper build can be the costlier choice.

title: 🔵 Universal Music vs Distrokid: beware the hidden agenda
role: Founder and MD, Motive Unknown (music marketing agency, UK); Network Notes
summary: Hemmings accepts that Universal Music's lawsuit against DistroKid targets a real problem, AI-generated tracks flooding streaming services, but argues the hidden aim is to weaken one of the few independent distribution pipes the majors do not control. Having lost the battle to own masters long term, he says, the majors are now pursuing a 'picks and shovels' strategy of owning the tools independents need, as Universal did when it pushed through zero payouts for tracks under 1,000 plays with little consultation. He wants AI music regulated, but by market regulators (most likely the EU), not steered by Universal.
why: A reminder that industry-wide fixes proposed by the dominant player can also be moves against its competitors.

limitations: Retail evidence, not sport. Figures are as Scaman gave them in November 2025; the sport application is Front Row's, not the author's.

bridge.insight: AI agents are becoming the gatekeeper between brands and customers; they reward verifiable delivery over messaging, and they serve whoever owns them (Scaman's talk and preface).
bridge.decision: A club, league or venue ticketing and digital lead deciding whether to expose ticket and merchandise inventory to AI agents, or keep checkout and fan data on its own channels.
bridge.adaptation: Fans are more loyal to a club than to most retail brands and event inventory is scarce and dated, so the risk is less substitution and more losing the fan relationship and data at the moment of purchase.
bridge.test: For one on-sale, track conversion and data capture by route (agent, search, own app). The analogy fails if fans keep buying direct for high-demand fixtures.

title: The Identity Shift
role: Strategist; writes Musings Of A Wandering Mind
summary: Scaman republishes her November 2025 IAA talk, The Identity Shift, with a new preface. Her argument: the relationship between brands and customers is starting to run through AI agents that read your data rather than your ads, and check claims against what a business actually delivers. She sets out three challenges (interface, data and authenticity) and sharpens one point: an agent works for whoever owns it, so when Meta takes a cut of purchases made through its Muse agent, the customer's and the platform's interests drift apart. She cites Walmart's finding that purchases completed inside ChatGPT converted at about a third of the rate of its own site.
why: Ticket, membership and merchandise journeys may start inside someone else's agent. Her test is who owns that agent and who keeps the customer relationship.

title: 183 - What Business Are You Really In?
role: Host, Sports Marketing Machine podcast; 21+ years in sports marketing
summary: In a solo episode recorded after a family loss, Neisser borrows a Chick-fil-A owner's line ('McDonald's is in the burger business, Chick-fil-A is in the community growing business') and argues teams are in the memory-making business. He applies it to campaigns: rewrite a '$12 tickets, buy now' promo around the experience it makes possible, and recognise the same game is bought four ways (family, date night, company outing, long-time season ticket holder).
why: A useful reframe for ticket and CRM teams, though this episode is about perspective rather than a tested tactic.
key_points: Segment by what fans want to experience, not just how to get them to buy.
Read a lapsed-buyer list as hundreds of life changes, not churn events, and write win-back emails accordingly.
Per-cap figures miss what a family actually bought with four tickets.

title: Somerset Sounds Out a New Summertime Revenue Stream... 🏟️
role: Managing Director, TPF Labs, The Players Fund; Sports Pundit
summary: Somerset County Cricket Club and Full Fat 360 are launching Somerset Sounds, an annual summer concert series at the County Ground from 2027, pitched as a fixture on the UK touring circuit rather than an occasional gig. Marston argues the timing is driven by the ECB's Hundred stake-sale payout to non-host counties, which must go on debt or long-term revenue projects, not player wages, and that the club can lean on a big membership base and a region with strong music demand but few concert venues.
why: A 145-year-old cricket ground turning spare summer capacity into a concert business shows traditional venues do not need a purpose-built stadium to add live music revenue.

title: UP572 Creators: What Are They Good For?
role: Owner and editor, Unofficial Partner
summary: Gillis talks to talent agent Jo Tongue and Lisa Parfitt of agency The Space Between about creators in sport, starting from the 'Wimbledon bans influencers' headline. What Wimbledon actually did was decline a creator accreditation category and confiscate ring lights under existing rules. Tongue puts responsibility for creator behaviour on whoever invited them. Parfitt cites research showing rights holder channels reach only about 27% of a sport's fans, and notes Unilever moving 50 to 70% of activation budgets to creators.
why: If owned channels reach about a quarter of fans, creators are a distribution question for rights holders and sponsors, not a nuisance to manage.
key_points: Agents now match talent to the outcome a brand wants, not just reach.
Heavy approval processes raise costs; brand risk after Callaway and Good Good is discussed.
Athletes face growing pressure to become creators themselves.
The Women's T20 World Cup used a 70/30 split between sport and lifestyle content.

title: Sports influencer marketing: what investors and growth companies should watch
role: Founder, Berkida Ventures; The Berkida Brief
summary: Drawing on OpenSponsorship founder Ishveen Jolly, Marinelli sets out how athlete and creator marketing becomes an investable, measurable business rather than relationship-driven deals. Every deal turns on four questions: who to pick, what to pay, how to execute the creative and how to prove the return. The best brands reuse creator assets in paid media, PR, connected TV and email, and A/B test them against generic content on acquisition cost. AI speeds up discovery but not pricing, negotiation or delivery. Female athletes made up 70% of OpenSponsorship's deals by number (not by value) in the latest year discussed.
why: A practical checklist for buying or selling athlete-creator partnerships on outcomes rather than follower counts.

title: Author Spencer Waller Joins Dave to Talk About The History of Antitrust and Monopolies in the Theater Business + What Does Rob Bonta's Surrender on ParaBros Merger Mean for Live Nation?
role: Senior Director, Live Music and Touring, Billboard; founder Decibel
summary: Antitrust professor and former DOJ prosecutor Spencer Weber Waller, author of 'Power and Greed', traces monopoly in live entertainment from the 1896 Theatrical Syndicate, which controlled Broadway houses and tour booking, to the Shuberts, who were forced in the 1950s to sell theatres and exit booking and ticketing. He argues enforcement usually arrives as a monopoly is already declining, that the breakup still improved Broadway, and that Live Nation arguably has more power than both. He calls the DOJ's mid-trial settlement lenient and says a breakup is the right remedy after two broken consent decrees.
why: A century of history that explains why regulators distrust behavioural promises from vertically integrated promoters, venues and ticketers.
key_points: Theatre escaped antitrust for decades because courts ruled it was not 'trade or commerce'.
The Syndicate brought order to chaotic touring but charged a heavy price for it; producers and venues could only work inside its system.
Brooks and Seville also argue California's Paramount-Warner settlement will carry little weight for Live Nation, which already broke earlier behavioural commitments.

title: The Kraken Had a Full Building…
role: Writes Talking Tickets!, a newsletter for people who sell tickets to live events: sports, concerts, opera and entertainment
summary: The Seattle Kraken were selling out Climate Pledge Arena, yet owner Samantha Holloway said fans found prices too high and promised a reset. Wakeman contrasts this with the Canucks, where upper-bowl seats with a $150 face value resell for a third of that or less. The Kraken's changes: shorter package commitments instead of 3 or 5 year terms, a $150 family-of-four package including food and soft drinks, a $10 item of the game and a $9.99 craft beer. He reads it as a deliberate bet on long-term fan relationships over 'number go up' pricing.
why: A concrete case of a sold-out team cutting entry prices to protect its future base, with the package mechanics spelled out.

title: On Signed Mbappé, One of Nike’s Biggest Athletes. Then He Went Back to Nike
role: Founder and publisher, Faze 3 Sport; Culture of Sport and Original Football
summary: Two days after being unveiled as the face of On's move into football, Kylian Mbappé played in Nike Mercurials with the Swoosh covered. Skilling likes the deal, especially Mbappé taking equity, but notes ownership makes an athlete harder to distance from if trouble arises. He questions why On hard-launched before its boot (due 2027) existed: the first match image was a rival's product, and Nike's customiser now lets fans recreate the white-on-white look. He contrasts Skechers, which unveiled Harry Kane and the boot together, with product on sale within weeks.
why: A useful counterpoint on athlete-equity deals and launch timing: a signing can solve the attention problem without solving the product problem.
